Muscles as Chemo-Electro-Mechanical Actuators

Module 5: how a nerve impulse becomes joint torque — from the calcium switch inside a sarcomere to a Hill-type model that turns a neural command into the force that lifts a bag, and fades when you tire.

Muscle force becomes joint torque through a geometric moment arm. The Achilles inserts on the calcaneus posterior to the ankle axis; $F_m$ times $d_m$ supplies plantarflexion torque.

0. Motivation — the force that has to be built

You reach down, grip a grocery bag, and lift it with your forearm horizontal. In Module 1 we solved the statics of exactly this pose: the elbow must supply a torque $\tau=F_m\,d_m$, and because the biceps inserts only about $d_m\approx3\ \mathrm{cm}$ from the joint while the bag hangs about $r_L\approx35\ \mathrm{cm}$ out along the forearm, torque balance forces the muscle to pull with roughly $F_m\approx(r_L/d_m)\,W\approx12\times$ the bag's weight — about $12\times(5\ \mathrm{kg})(9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}})\approx590\ \mathrm N$ if a single muscle at the $3\ \mathrm{cm}$ arm carried the whole load. The human arm is a third-class lever: it trades force for reach and speed, and the muscle pays the tax.

But Module 1 took that muscle force as given — a number that simply appears on the free-body diagram. Module 3 was even more explicit: when it set up the joint as a constrained mechanical interface, it left the applied muscle force $Q$ as a literal blank, a placeholder to be filled by "a Hill-type muscle with force–length–velocity behaviour, activation dynamics, and pennation." This module fills that blank. Where does the pulling force come from, what sets its size, and why can the nervous system dial it up and down at will?

The moment you ask, the cable picture falls apart — a muscle is nothing like a rope you can pull tight on demand:

  • It has a rise time. Decide to lift and the force does not appear instantly; it ramps up over roughly a tenth of a second, and it lingers briefly after you "let go." Force lags the command.
  • It depends on length. The same muscle that easily holds $5\ \mathrm{kg}$ with the elbow near a right angle can barely produce force when fully stretched or fully bunched up.
  • It depends on speed. Try to shorten quickly and the muscle weakens; resist while being forcibly lengthened (lowering the bag) and it is stronger than when still.
  • It fatigues. Hold the bag long enough and the very same neural command yields less and less force.

A cable does none of these things. Any honest account of "muscle force" has to reproduce all four — a rise time, a length dependence, a velocity dependence, and fatigue. Each is a clue about the machinery underneath, and each becomes a term in the model we build.

The resolution is the idea in the module's title: a muscle is a chemo-electro-mechanical actuator. A command that begins as a nerve signal is transduced — electrically, then chemically, then mechanically — into force, through a short chain of steps, each of which we can write down and quantify. It is cleanest to picture the whole module as a single pipeline:

To make each arrow quantitative we need three layers of physics, each built on the one before:

  • The generator itself — how muscle is built (fascicles, pennation, and the maximal force set by cross-sectional area), and the sarcomere, whose overlapping filaments give the force its dependence on length (§1–§2).
  • Turning a command into activation — the action potential at the neuromuscular junction, the calcium release that switches the machinery on, and how the nervous system grades whole-muscle drive by recruiting motor units and firing them faster — all collapsed into a first-order activation equation (§3–§5).
  • The force laws and the whole model — the dependence of force on shortening velocity (Hill's hyperbola), assembled with length and activation into the Hill-type muscle model, then converted to joint torque through a moment arm that varies with angle, with agonist and antagonist acting across the joint (§6–§8).

Two computational labs then put the model to work — predicting joint torque from a neural command through a movement, and showing how that torque fades under sustained effort (§9) — before we take honest stock of what the model captures and misses and close with problems (§10). By the end you will be able to hand the model a neural command and get back the torque it produces at the joint, moment by moment, and understand why the same command produces less when the muscle is tired. Every model in this module sits on Level 5 of the course's level ladder (muscle–tendon actuator models): a lumped actuator with activation dynamics and force–length–velocity laws, driving a joint through a moment arm. The labs of §9 prescribe the joint trajectory rather than integrating the limb, so nothing here is a Level‑2 planar rigid-body result; K7 takes the single step into Level 2 and shows what changes. We begin with the hardware: how a muscle is built to make force.

1. Muscle architecture: the force-producing hierarchy

Before we can ask how a nerve signal controls force (§3–§5), we need to know what sets the force a muscle can produce at all. That ceiling is fixed by architecture — how the tissue is built and arranged. So begin by zooming in, from the whole muscle you can see under the skin down to the molecular unit that actually generates tension.

A skeletal muscle is a nested bundle. Define each level of the hierarchy the first time it appears:

  • A whole muscle (say the biceps) is wrapped in connective tissue and tapers at each end into a tendon — the tough cord that transmits its force to bone.
  • Inside, the muscle is divided into fascicles: visible bundles of fibres, each sheathed in connective tissue (the perimysium). The arrangement of these fascicles relative to the tendon is what we will call pennation, below.
  • Each fascicle is a bundle of muscle fibres. A muscle fibre is a single cell — unusually, a long, cylindrical, multinucleated one (10–100 μm across, up to many centimetres long), striped (striated) with a regular cross-banding.
  • Each fibre is packed with hundreds of myofibrils: thread-like strands running its full length.
  • Each myofibril is a chain of sarcomeres laid end to end. The sarcomere is the contractile unit — the smallest piece that shortens and pulls. Its banding is the source of the fibre's stripes, and its internal machinery (thick and thin filaments) is where force is generated, developed in §2.

Two architectural numbers set the maximal force. First, how much contractile material the muscle carries across its section. Second, at what angle the fibres pull on the tendon. Take them in turn.

Specific tension and physiological cross-section

Every fibre is built from the same molecular machinery (the crossbridges of §2), packed at nearly the same density. So the force a fibre can exert is set simply by how many filaments lie side by side across its cross-section — i.e. by its cross-sectional area. The proportionality constant is a material property of muscle:

Definition 1.1 (specific tension). The specific tension $\sigma$ is the maximal isometric ("iso" = same, "metric" = length: contracting at fixed length) force a muscle produces per unit cross-sectional area of fibre. It is a stress (force / area), and across mammalian skeletal muscle it varies by less than a factor of two, $$\sigma \approx 0.3\ \mathrm{MPa} = 30\ \mathrm{N\,cm^{-2}},\tag{1.1}$$ with a measured range of about $0.2$–$0.35\ \mathrm{MPa}$. Its near-universality is the first hint that all muscle runs on one shared mechanism.

But a fibre in a pennate muscle does not run straight down the muscle's long axis, so the muscle's anatomical cross-section (a cut perpendicular to the whole muscle) slices fibres obliquely and undercounts them. The area that matters is the one taken perpendicular to the fibres themselves, summed over every fibre:

Definition 1.2 (physiological cross-sectional area, PCSA). The physiological cross-sectional area is the total cross-sectional area of all the muscle's fibres, measured perpendicular to their length. Since a bundle of fibres of length $L_f$ and total volume $V$ satisfies $V = \mathrm{PCSA}\times L_f$, $$\mathrm{PCSA} = \frac{V}{L_f} = \frac{m}{\rho\,L_f},\tag{1.2}$$ where $m$ is muscle mass and $\rho\approx1.06\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ is muscle density. PCSA counts contractile material, not girth: a fat muscle of long fibres can have a smaller PCSA than a slim muscle of short, densely packed ones.

The force a muscle's fibres generate along their own direction is then just specific tension times the physiological cross-section, $F_{\text{fibre}} = \sigma\,\mathrm{PCSA}$. What reaches the tendon depends on the pennation angle, which we quantify next.

Pennation: angling the fibres

Definition 1.3 (pennation angle). The pennation angle $\theta_p$ is the angle between a muscle's fibres and its tendon (its line of action). A muscle whose fibres run parallel to the tendon ($\theta_p\approx0$) is parallel (or fusiform); one whose fibres attach obliquely, like the barbs of a feather (Latin penna), is pennate.

Angling the fibres has an immediate mechanical cost: only the component of a fibre's force along the tendon actually pulls on the bone. Resolve the fibre force $F_{\text{fibre}}$ into a component along the tendon and one perpendicular to it:

So each fibre delivers $F_{\text{fibre}}\cos\theta_p$ along the tendon (eq. below). This looks like a pure loss — yet the most powerful muscles in the body (the quadriceps, the calf) are strongly pennate. The resolution is a trade-off: angling the fibres frees up room, so a pennate muscle can pack many more (necessarily shorter) fibres into the same volume. By (1.2), halving the fibre length doubles the PCSA. That gain in PCSA scales faster than the modest $\cos\theta_p$ loss (at $\theta_p=25^\circ$, $\cos\theta_p=0.91$ — only a 9% cut), so pennate muscles are high-force designs. The price they pay is elsewhere: short fibres shorten by only a short distance, so pennate muscles have small range and high force, while parallel muscles have large range and lower force. Architecture is a choice between force and excursion.

Collecting the two effects gives the maximal isometric force a muscle delivers to its tendon:

Proposition 1.1 (maximal isometric force from architecture). A muscle of specific tension $\sigma$, physiological cross-sectional area $\mathrm{PCSA}$, and pennation angle $\theta_p$ delivers a maximal isometric tendon force $$\boxed{\;F_{\max} \;=\; \sigma\,\mathrm{PCSA}\,\cos\theta_p\;}\tag{1.3}$$ This is the ceiling the neural control of §3–§7 can approach but never exceed; every later force term is a fraction of it.
By Definition 1.1 the specific tension $\sigma$ is force per unit fibre cross-section, so the fibres' summed maximal force along their own axis is $\sigma\times\mathrm{PCSA}$ — Definition 1.2 defined $\mathrm{PCSA}$ as exactly the cross-section perpendicular to the fibres, the area this stress acts on. But that axial force is not what reaches the bone: by the force triangle of Fig. 4 each fibre delivers only its tendon-directed component $F_{\text{fibre}}\cos\theta_p$ (Definition 1.3). Since every fibre is inclined at the same $\theta_p$, projecting the whole array onto the tendon multiplies the axial total by the one common factor $\cos\theta_p$, giving $F_{\max}=\sigma\,\mathrm{PCSA}\,\cos\theta_p$. ∎

Put in numbers. With $\sigma=30\ \mathrm{N\,cm^{-2}}$, a muscle's maximal force in newtons is just $30\times\mathrm{PCSA}\,[\mathrm{cm^2}]\times\cos\theta_p$. The table spans the range from a small parallel flexor to the big pennate extensors. Its PCSA and pennation values are representative measured figures for an adult (Appendix); $F_{\max}$ in the last column is computed from them by (1.3):

MusclePCSA (cm²)Pennation $\theta_p$Architecture$F_{\max}=\sigma\,\mathrm{PCSA}\cos\theta_p$ (N)
Biceps brachii~4.5~0° (parallel)long fibres, large range~135
Gastrocnemius~30~17°pennate~860
Soleus~50~25°strongly pennate, short fibres~1360
Quadriceps (four heads)~150~12°large, pennate~4400

Validation against §0. In §0 holding a $5\ \mathrm{kg}$ bag on a horizontal forearm demanded an elbow torque $\tau=W\,r_L\approx(49\ \mathrm N)(0.35\ \mathrm m)\approx17\ \mathrm{N\,m}$ — equivalently $\approx590\ \mathrm N$ of pull if a single muscle carried it all at the $3\ \mathrm{cm}$ biceps arm. Now check that against architecture. The biceps alone reaches only $F_{\max}\approx135\ \mathrm N$; but it is one of several flexors — the bulkier brachialis ($\mathrm{PCSA}\approx7\ \mathrm{cm^2}$, so $\sigma\,\mathrm{PCSA}\approx210\ \mathrm N$) and the brachioradialis add more, for a group pull of several hundred newtons. Two things then close the apparent gap to $590\ \mathrm N$: that figure is a single-muscle-equivalent, and the real flexors act at a spread of moment arms — the brachioradialis inserts far out along the forearm, so the group balances the $17\ \mathrm{N\,m}$ with less total force than a lone $3\ \mathrm{cm}$-arm muscle would need. Order of magnitude matches; exact closure would need each muscle's own moment arm. And the demand is well inside the group's ceiling: a maximal isometric elbow flexion is tens of newton-metres (roughly $50$–$80\ \mathrm{N\,m}$), so $17\ \mathrm{N\,m}$ is a firm but distinctly submaximal effort — sustainable, yet fatiguing over time, not the flexors' limit. The calf and thigh numbers ($\sim10^3\ \mathrm N$) likewise match the joint reactions of Module 3, where standing loaded the hip to $\sim1700\ \mathrm N$.

Equation (1.3) fixes the size of the force. But a muscle almost never works at $F_{\max}$: the force it actually makes depends on how stretched it is, how fast it is shortening, and how strongly it is switched on. The first of these — the dependence on length — is written into the very geometry of the sarcomere we just drew, and it is where we turn next (§2).

2. The sarcomere: crossbridges and the length–tension law

Section 1 fixed the ceiling on force, $F_{\max}=\sigma\,\mathrm{PCSA}\cos\theta_p$. But a muscle almost never delivers $F_{\max}$. The force it actually produces at any instant is that ceiling scaled by three dimensionless factors, each between 0 and 1:

$F_{\text{active}} \;=\; \underbrace{a(t)}_{\text{how switched on}}\;\cdot\; \underbrace{f_L(\ell)}_{\text{how stretched}}\;\cdot\; \underbrace{f_V(v)}_{\text{how fast}}\;\cdot\; F_{\max}$

Activation $a$ is the story of §3–§5; the velocity factor $f_V$ is §6. This section derives the middle one — the length factor $f_L(\ell)$ — and the remarkable thing is that it falls straight out of the geometry of the sarcomere we already drew in §1 (Fig. 3). Force is made by molecular crossbridges; a crossbridge can only pull where a thin filament lies beside it; how much thin filament lies beside the bridges is set by how long the sarcomere is. So force must depend on length — and we can compute exactly how.

The sliding-filament model

Recall the sarcomere from §1: central thick (myosin) filaments interdigitating with thin (actin) filaments anchored to the Z-discs at each end. Define the one length this section turns on:

Definition 2.1 (sarcomere length). The sarcomere length $\ell$ is the distance between the two Z-discs that bound one sarcomere — the length of the repeating contractile unit. At rest in human muscle $\ell\approx2.6$–$2.8\ \mu\mathrm m$.

How does a muscle shorten? Not by the filaments themselves getting shorter. In the sliding-filament model (A. F. Huxley and Hanson, 1954) the thick and thin filaments keep their lengths and instead slide past one another: the thin filaments are drawn deeper in between the thick ones, hauling the Z-discs together and shrinking $\ell$. The tell-tale evidence is that the thick-filament band stays a fixed width under the microscope while the sarcomere shortens — only the overlap changes. Everything below follows from that one fact. (An animation of this sliding is the capstone figure of the section, once we know what it does to force.)

The crossbridge cycle — where force and ATP meet

Projecting from each thick filament are hundreds of myosin heads, or crossbridges: tiny motor domains that reach out, grab the neighbouring thin filament, and pull. Each head runs a four-state cycle, burning exactly one molecule of ATP (adenosine triphosphate, the cell's energy currency) per turn (Fig. 5):

Two consequences matter for the rest of the module. First, one ATP is hydrolysed per crossbridge per cycle — the chemical price of the mechanical work, the "chemo-" in this module's title. Second, and more immediately, the heads act as a parallel array of tiny, independent force generators: at any instant the sarcomere's active force is the sum of the pulls of all the heads that happen to be attached, so

active force $\;\propto\;$ number of crossbridges attached at that instant.

What one stroke costs, and what one ATP can pay

“One ATP per cycle” is a price, and Module 0 §3 has put a number on it. The free energy released by hydrolysing one mole of ATP in a living muscle is not the tabulated standard value but $\Delta G = \Delta G^{\circ\prime} + R_gT\ln Q$ evaluated at the cell’s own composition (with $\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$ the standard free energy at pH 7 and $Q = [\mathrm{ADP}][\mathrm{P_i}]/[\mathrm{ATP}]$ the reaction quotient at that composition), and the composition moves during work: $\Delta G = -62.5\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ in resting muscle and $-52.7\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ at the end of a fatiguing bout, the whole difference being the concentration term as phosphate accumulates. (Here $T$ is absolute temperature and $R_g$ the gas constant, as in Module 0; this $T$ is not the blocked troponin unit that the proof of Proposition 3.1 in §3 uses locally.) Per molecule, dividing by Avogadro’s number $N_A$ and by the thermal energy $k_BT = 4.28\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm J$ at $37\ ^\circ\mathrm C$, one ATP is worth $24.2\,k_BT$ at rest and $20.4\,k_BT$ when fatigued.

Against that budget set the work one stroke delivers. A head pulling with force $f_{\text{head}}$ through its stroke $d\approx10\ \mathrm{nm}$ does non-expansion work $W_{\text{ne}} = f_{\text{head}}\,d$ (written $W_{\text{ne}}$ rather than $W$, because $W$ is the bag’s weight in §0). Single-molecule measurements put $f_{\text{head}}$ at $3$–$6\ \mathrm{pN}$; at $5\ \mathrm{pN}$ the stroke work is $5\times10^{-20}\ \mathrm J = 11.7\,k_BT$. Module 0’s maximum-work theorem (its Proposition 3.1, $W_{\text{ne}}\le-\Delta G$) then does two things at once. It caps the average force a head can exert over its stroke at $|\Delta G|/(N_A d)$, which is $10.38\ \mathrm{pN}$ resting and $8.75\ \mathrm{pN}$ fatigued (Module 0 prints $8.76$ from its unrounded $\Delta G$) — both above the measured $3$–$6\ \mathrm{pN}$, so the ceiling is real but never binding, and fatigue is not the ceiling descending onto the head (Module 0 §3 says why: the measured force loss comes from phosphate acting on the cycle itself). And it defines the crossbridge efficiency, the fraction of one ATP’s free energy that leaves as work:

$$\eta_{\text{xb}} \;=\; \frac{f_{\text{head}}\,d\,N_A}{|\Delta G|} \;=\; \begin{cases}0.48 & \text{resting muscle},\\[2pt] 0.57 & \text{end of a hard bout}\end{cases}\qquad(f_{\text{head}} = 5\ \mathrm{pN},\ d = 10\ \mathrm{nm}),$$

with the range $0.29$–$0.58$ at rest across the measured $3$–$6\ \mathrm{pN}$. The fatigued efficiency is higher only because the denominator has shrunk: the same stroke work is a larger fraction of a cheaper ATP. An efficiency near one half is what a well-designed motor at the molecular scale looks like — the rest of the free energy is dissipated as heat in the irreversible steps of the cycle, exactly the shortfall from equality that Module 0’s theorem allows for.

The ATP ledger, per head. Bars in units of $k_BT$ at $37\ ^\circ\mathrm C$: one ATP at Module 0’s two measured compositions (green) against the work of one $10\ \mathrm{nm}$ stroke at three measured head forces (red). No red bar reaches a green one, which is the maximum-work theorem holding; at $5\ \mathrm{pN}$ the stroke spends about half the ATP, and the thermodynamic ceiling on the force lies well above what a head actually exerts.

Not every ATP a muscle splits reaches a crossbridge. Ending the contraction costs ATP too: §3 will meet the SERCA pump, which returns two calcium ions to the sarcoplasmic reticulum (the fibre’s internal calcium store) per ATP (Module 0 §3 shows that three is thermodynamically forbidden in a working muscle), and the sodium pump that restores the membrane after each impulse. Measured on whole fibres, these pumps take a fraction $\phi_{\text{pump}}\approx0.30$–$0.40$ of the ATP turned over in a contraction. The muscle’s mechanical efficiency is therefore bounded by $\eta_{\text{xb}}(1-\phi_{\text{pump}}) = 0.29$–$0.34$ at rest. A whole muscle approaches that bound only at its best shortening speed. An isometric hold does no external work at any efficiency, and at every other speed a stroke delivers less than $f_{\text{head}}\,d$ (§6). The $20$–$25\%$ quoted for whole-body exercise sits below this bound because it also carries the efficiency of making the ATP in the first place, which belongs to the energetics of locomotion (Modules 8 and 9), not to this ledger.

The same ledger, run per unit area instead of per head, says where the specific tension $\sigma$ of §1 comes from:

Lemma 2.1 (specific tension from the crossbridge ledger). Let a fibre hold $n_{\text{fil}}$ thick filaments per unit cross-sectional area of myofibril, each with $N_{\text{half}}$ heads per half-filament; let a fraction $\phi_{\text{att}}$ of those heads be attached at the instant of peak force in a maximal isometric contraction, each bearing $f_{\text{head}}$; and let myofibrils occupy a fraction $\chi$ of the fibre’s cross-section. Then the maximal isometric force per unit fibre area is $$\sigma \;=\; \chi\,n_{\text{fil}}\,N_{\text{half}}\,\phi_{\text{att}}\,f_{\text{head}}.$$
Every half-sarcomere along a myofibril is in series, so the force through each is the same and equals the sum of the pulls of its attached heads, by the parallel-array picture above: $N_{\text{half}}\phi_{\text{att}}f_{\text{head}}$ per thick filament. Thick filaments across the myofibril’s cross-section act in parallel, so their forces add: $n_{\text{fil}}$ per unit area gives $n_{\text{fil}}N_{\text{half}}\phi_{\text{att}}f_{\text{head}}$ per unit myofibril area. Only the fraction $\chi$ of the fibre’s section is myofibril, the rest being mitochondria, reticulum and cytosol that bear no active load, which scales the force per unit fibre area by $\chi$. Where the hypotheses bind: the heads must be independent (Modelling assumption 2.2 below), and $\phi_{\text{att}}$ must be the attached fraction at the instant of peak force, not the average over a cycle. ∎

Put in numbers from structure. X-ray diffraction gives the thick-filament lattice spacing $d_{10}\approx38\ \mathrm{nm}$ at rest length, which in a hexagonal lattice is one filament per $1670\ \mathrm{nm^2}$, $n_{\text{fil}} = 6.0\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{m^{-2}}$; a thick filament carries $294$ heads, so $N_{\text{half}} = 147$; myofibrils fill $\chi\approx0.83$ of a fibre. The two remaining inputs are the least certain, and the answer is only as good as they are: at $f_{\text{head}} = 5\ \mathrm{pN}$ and $\phi_{\text{att}} = 0.3$ the lemma gives $\sigma = 11\ \mathrm{N\,cm^{-2}}$; at $6\ \mathrm{pN}$ and $0.4$ it gives $17.6$; at $5\ \mathrm{pN}$ and $0.5$, $18.3$. The measured $20$–$35\ \mathrm{N\,cm^{-2}}$ of §1 is therefore accounted for to within a factor of two to three by counting heads, and the shortfall lives entirely in the attached fraction and the force per head.

measured, not derived: the specific tension $\sigma = 30\ \mathrm{N\,cm^{-2}}$ behind every $F_{\max}$ in this module is a fibre measurement. Lemma 2.1 reproduces its order of magnitude from filament spacing and head count, but its two decisive inputs are not independent of the measurement they are checking: the force per head is measured on isolated molecules in an optical trap (a focused laser that holds a bead and reads piconewton forces from its displacement), and the attached fraction $\phi_{\text{att}}$ is inferred from fibre stiffness and X-ray intensity in the same maximally activated fibres whose tension is being explained. A $\sigma$ built from those inputs is a consistency check on the molecular picture, not a prediction of the tissue number, and this module keeps $\sigma$ as the measured input it always was.

Force follows overlap

A head can only attach where there is a thin filament beside it to grab. The heads are spread (at nearly uniform density) along the thick filament everywhere except a central bare zone that carries no heads. So the number of heads that can attach is set by how much thin filament lies alongside the head-bearing part of the thick filament — the overlap. To turn "∝ attached heads" into "∝ overlap length" we make one modelling assumption explicit, because it is exactly what makes the derivation work:

Modelling assumption 2.2 (independent, uniform crossbridges). The myosin heads are (i) distributed at uniform density along the head-bearing zones of the thick filament, and (ii) independent and identical force generators. Then the number of attachable heads — and hence the active force — is proportional to the length of overlap between the thin filaments and the head-bearing zone: $$F_{\text{active}} \;\propto\; (\text{overlap length}).\tag{2.1}$$ Uniform density is what makes this proportionality linear; it is the hinge of the whole length–tension law.

Sarcomere geometry sets the curve

Now it is pure bookkeeping of lengths. Take representative human filament dimensions (each varies a little between muscles and people — the spread is given):

SymbolQuantityValue (representative human)
$A$thick (myosin) filament length$1.60\ \mu\mathrm m$
$a_{\text{thin}}$thin (actin) filament length, one side (from the Z-line)$\approx 1.3\ \mu\mathrm m$ (range $1.27$–$1.32$)
$B$central bare zone (head-free) width$\approx 0.1$–$0.2\ \mu\mathrm m$
$\tfrac{A-B}{2}$head-bearing length, one side$\approx 0.75\ \mu\mathrm m$

Watch the overlap change as we lengthen the sarcomere from fully shortened to fully stretched. Four snapshots (Fig. 6) tell the whole story (the force under each is computed from (2.1)):

Each snapshot is a breakpoint of the curve, and each is a clean statement about lengths (all measured Z-to-Z). Reading from long to short:

  • Descending-limb zero — the thin filaments have slid completely clear of the thick filament, so overlap and force reach zero. This happens when the sarcomere length equals the thick length plus both thin filaments: $\ell = A + 2\,a_{\text{thin}} = 1.60 + 2(1.30) = 4.20\ \mu\mathrm m.$
  • Plateau (optimal length $\ell_0$) — as the sarcomere shortens from there, overlap grows until every head is engaged. That is first true when the thin-filament tips just reach the edge of the bare zone: $\ell_0 = 2\,a_{\text{thin}} + B = 2.60 + 0.10 = 2.70\ \mu\mathrm m.$ Shorten a touch more and the thin tips slide across the (head-free) bare zone without gaining or losing any engaged heads — so force stays flat until the tips meet at the centre, at $\ell = 2\,a_{\text{thin}} = 2.60\ \mu\mathrm m$. The plateau width equals the bare-zone width $B$: the head-free centre is exactly what buys a muscle a range of lengths at full force.
  • Ascending limb — below $2.60\ \mu\mathrm m$ the thin filaments overshoot the centre and enter the opposite half, where they lie the wrong way among the far heads and interfere (the orange double overlap); force declines. At $\ell = A = 1.60\ \mu\mathrm m$ the thick filaments run into the Z-discs and begin to crumple, and force drops steeply, extrapolating to zero near $\ell\approx1.27\ \mu\mathrm m$.

That last zero deserves a caution. Unlike the descending limb — whose zero at $4.2\ \mu\mathrm m$ is pure thin/thick geometry — the ascending zero near $1.27\ \mu\mathrm m$ is an empirical extrapolation set by the thick filament buckling against the Z-discs, a property of the (nearly species-invariant) thick filament rather than a length we can derive by overlap alone. So we treat the descending limb and plateau as exact geometry and the ascending limb as a measured, piecewise-linear approximation. The figures draw it with two slopes (steep below $1.6\ \mu\mathrm m$, shallow above); the lab scripts later in this module use one straight line from $1.27$ to $2.60\ \mu\mathrm m$, a simpler fit of the same limb.

Collecting all four regions gives the active length–tension law — the first mechanical law of the module:

Proposition 2.1 (active length–tension relation). With sarcomere length $\ell$ in micrometres, the normalized active force is $$\boxed{\;f_L(\ell)=\begin{cases}0, & \ell\le 1.27 \ \text{ or }\ \ell\ge 4.20,\\[3pt]\text{ascending (double overlap; thick-filament}\\[-1pt]\quad\text{compression) }\nearrow, & 1.27\lt\ell\lt2.60,\\[3pt]1, & 2.60\le\ell\le 2.70\quad(\text{plateau}),\\[3pt]\dfrac{4.20-\ell}{4.20-2.70}, & 2.70\lt\ell\lt4.20.\end{cases}\;}$$ The plateau sits at the optimal length $\ell_0\approx2.7\ \mu\mathrm m$; force falls to zero at $\ell\approx1.27$ and $4.20\ \mu\mathrm m$.
(Four regions from filament overlap.) The three breakpoints were read off the filament lengths above: the descending zero at $\ell=A+2a_{\text{thin}}=4.20\ \mu\mathrm m$ (thin filaments clear of the thick), the plateau across $2.60$–$2.70\ \mu\mathrm m$ (its width is exactly the bare-zone $B$), and the ascending decline below $2.60\ \mu\mathrm m$. Only the descending slope is left to fix. On the descending limb every attached head lies in the head-bearing zone, and by (2.1) force is proportional to the overlap between one thin filament and one head-bearing half of the thick filament. Measuring from the sarcomere centre, that half runs out to $A/2$, and the thin filament's inner tip sits at $\ell/2 - a_{\text{thin}}$, so $$\text{overlap}(\ell) \;=\; \frac{A}{2} - \Big(\frac{\ell}{2} - a_{\text{thin}}\Big),$$ which shrinks linearly as $\ell$ grows. Normalising by its maximum, the head-bearing length $\tfrac{A-B}{2}=0.75\ \mu\mathrm m$, gives the straight descending limb $\dfrac{4.20-\ell}{4.20-2.70}$, running from $f_L=1$ at $\ell_0=2.70$ to $f_L=0$ at $4.20\ \mu\mathrm m$. The plateau and descending limb are thus exact filament geometry; the ascending limb (double overlap, then thick-filament compression against the Z-discs) is the measured piecewise-linear approximation flagged above, and $f_L=0$ outside $[1.27,\,4.20]$. ∎

Plotted, the law is the classic humped curve (Fig. 7):

This is A. F. Huxley's overlap prediction, confirmed in the landmark single-fibre experiments of Gordon, Huxley & Julian (1966): the measured force tracks the computed overlap breakpoint-for-breakpoint. Our three landmarks match the human values quoted at the start — plateau at $\ell_0\approx2.7\ \mu\mathrm m$, zeros near $1.27$ and $4.2\ \mu\mathrm m$ — a geometry-only prediction validated against measurement.

What does it mean for a working muscle? Sarcomeres in the body are held, by their tendons and skeletal geometry, to operate mostly on the plateau and the near flanks around $\ell_0$ — they rarely wander out to the zeros, where they would be useless. But they do move off the plateau: this is why your grip is weakest with the wrist fully flexed or fully extended (finger-flexor sarcomeres pushed onto the ascending or descending limb), and strongest in between. The animation (Fig. 8) makes the link concrete — as the sarcomere breathes through its length range, watch the operating point ride up and down the very curve we just derived:

Two loose ends, both repaid later. The velocity factor $f_V(v)$ — force also depends on how fast the filaments are sliding, because the crossbridge cycle takes time — is §6. And the sharp corners of the single-sarcomere curve above are rounded off in a whole muscle, because its millions of sarcomeres are never all at exactly the same length; the smoothed, normalised fibre-level $f_L$ that §7 plugs into the Hill model is this curve with its kinks averaged away. With length handled, we turn to the switch that decides how many of these crossbridges are active at all: the calcium signal of §3.

3. Excitation–contraction coupling: from action potential to calcium

Section 2 taught that a crossbridge pulls only where a thin filament lies beside it. But it needs one more thing: the actin binding site must be exposed. At rest those sites are physically covered, so even a sarcomere at optimal overlap, flush with ATP, makes no force. Overlap is necessary but not sufficient — the muscle also needs a go signal.

That signal is calcium, dumped into the muscle cell the instant the motor nerve fires. Tracing how a nerve impulse becomes a calcium pulse is the electro- of this "chemo-electro-mechanical" module, and it hands us the last missing quantity: activation $a$ — the dimensionless switch, between 0 and 1, that §5 will model as an ODE and §7 will multiply into the force. The whole cascade, nerve to filament, is one figure (Fig. 9):

The neuromuscular junction: nerve impulse to muscle impulse

A skeletal muscle fibre is commanded by exactly one motor neuron, which meets it at the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) — the synapse between nerve and muscle. When an action potential (a self-propagating wave of membrane depolarisation) reaches the nerve terminal, it opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels there; the inrushing Ca²⁺ triggers release of the neurotransmitter acetylcholine (ACh) into the narrow synaptic cleft. ACh binds receptors on the motor end-plate (the specialised patch of muscle membrane under the terminal), opening ion channels that depolarise it.

That depolarisation is large enough to ignite a fresh, all-or-none muscle action potential in the sarcolemma (the muscle fibre's cell membrane), which then races along the fibre in both directions at a few metres per second. The NMJ is a high-safety-factor relay: unlike the many-to-one synapses of the brain, one nerve impulse reliably yields exactly one muscle impulse. So the CNS controls a fibre entirely by when and how often it fires — a fact §4 builds on.

From voltage to calcium: the T-tubule and the sarcoplasmic reticulum

To reach the contractile machinery packed throughout the fibre's interior, the muscle action potential travels down the T-tubules — tubular invaginations of the sarcolemma that plunge deep into the cell, carrying the voltage signal inward. Each T-tubule runs alongside the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR), an internal membrane sac that stores Ca²⁺ at high concentration. Where a T-tubule meets two SR sacs sits the triad, and there the coupling happens:

  • Embedded in the T-tubule membrane is the voltage sensor DHPR (the dihydropyridine receptor). When the action potential's voltage reaches it, the DHPR changes shape.
  • The DHPR is physically tethered to the RyR (ryanodine receptor), the Ca²⁺-release channel in the SR membrane. The DHPR's conformational change mechanically pulls the RyR open.

This mechanical gating is the signature of skeletal muscle: the voltage sensor opens the release channel by direct physical linkage, not by calcium triggering more calcium (the calcium-induced-calcium-release mechanism of cardiac muscle). The instant the RyR opens, Ca²⁺ floods from the SR into the cytosol, and the free calcium concentration leaps from its resting $\sim0.1\ \mu\mathrm M$ to $\sim1$–$2\ \mu\mathrm M$ within a few milliseconds.

The pulse is transient because the SR immediately fights to reclaim its calcium. Studded through the SR membrane is the SERCA pump (a Ca²⁺-ATPase) that spends one ATP to drag Ca²⁺ back inside — another entry in the module's chemical-energy ledger. Release then re-uptake makes the calcium transient: a sharp rise as the RyR dumps Ca²⁺, and a decay of tens of milliseconds as SERCA pumps it away.

Where the voltage comes from: Nernst, the constant-field equation, and the cost of excitability

The action potential has so far been narrated — a depolarisation that “sweeps” the membrane — and the voltages in it have been taken as given. They are not free parameters. Module 0 §5 derives, from the equality of electrochemical potential across a membrane (its Proposition 5.2, the Nernst equation), the one voltage at which an ion has no net tendency to cross: $$E_i \;=\; \frac{R_gT}{z_iF_{\text{Far}}}\ln\frac{c_{i,\text{out}}}{c_{i,\text{in}}},\qquad \frac{R_gT}{F_{\text{Far}}} = 26.73\ \mathrm{mV}\ \text{at}\ 37\ ^\circ\mathrm C,$$ where $z_i$ is the ion’s valence, $c_i$ its concentration ($c$ is a concentration in this subsection only; the Hill curvature $c$ of §6 is a dimensionless number), and $F_{\text{Far}} = 96\,485\ \mathrm{C\,mol^{-1}}$ is the Faraday constant — written with its subscript in this module because $F$ is muscle force everywhere else in it, exactly the collision Module 0 §5 warned of. (The symbol $E_i$ is a potential, not a modulus.) For a skeletal-muscle fibre, with the interstitial and cytosolic concentrations Module 0 tabulates (outside/inside, in mM: K $4/140$, Na $145/12$, Cl $116/4$, Ca $1.8/0.0001$), the four values are $E_{\mathrm K} = -95.0$, $E_{\mathrm{Na}} = +66.6$, $E_{\mathrm{Cl}} = -90.0$ and $E_{\mathrm{Ca}} = +130.9\ \mathrm{mV}$. A resting fibre sits near $-90\ \mathrm{mV}$: close to potassium and chloride, and $157\ \mathrm{mV}$ away from sodium. That gap is the stored energy an impulse spends.

A membrane permeable to several ions settles not at any one Nernst potential but at a compromise weighted by how permeable it is to each. That compromise has a closed form under one idealisation, and it is the equation every voltage in this section rests on:

Lemma 3.1 (the Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz potential). Let a membrane of thickness $L$ separate solutions of the monovalent ions $\mathrm{K^+}$, $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$; let each ion cross independently, by diffusion and by drift in the field, with permeability $P_i$; and assume the electric field inside the membrane is uniform (the constant-field assumption). Then the membrane potential $V = \phi_{\text{in}}-\phi_{\text{out}}$ (a voltage, not the muscle volume $V$ of §1; and $\phi$ is the electric potential, as in Module 0 Definition 5.3, not the fractions $\phi_{\text{pump}}$, $\phi_{\text{att}}$ of §2) at which the total ionic current vanishes is $$\boxed{\;V \;=\; \frac{R_gT}{F_{\text{Far}}}\ln\frac{P_{\mathrm K}[\mathrm K^+]_{\text{out}} + P_{\mathrm{Na}}[\mathrm{Na}^+]_{\text{out}} + P_{\mathrm{Cl}}[\mathrm{Cl}^-]_{\text{in}}}{P_{\mathrm K}[\mathrm K^+]_{\text{in}} + P_{\mathrm{Na}}[\mathrm{Na}^+]_{\text{in}} + P_{\mathrm{Cl}}[\mathrm{Cl}^-]_{\text{out}}}\;}$$ Only the ratios of the permeabilities matter, and with a single permeant ion the expression collapses to that ion’s Nernst potential.
Take the $x$ axis across the membrane from $x=0$ (outside) to $x=L$ (inside), and write $u = F_{\text{Far}}V/(R_gT)$ for the dimensionless potential. The flux of an ion of valence $z$ (moles per area per time, positive inward) is the Nernst–Planck flux, diffusion plus drift down the electrochemical gradient of Module 0 Definition 5.3: $$J \;=\; -D\left(\frac{\mathrm dc}{\mathrm dx} + z\,c\,\frac{F_{\text{Far}}}{R_gT}\frac{\mathrm d\phi}{\mathrm dx}\right),$$ with $D$ the ion’s diffusion coefficient inside the membrane, and $u$ local to this proof (the neural drive of §4 also uses the letter). With a uniform field, $\mathrm d\phi/\mathrm dx = V/L$, this is a first-order linear equation in $c(x)$ with constant coefficients, $c' + (zu/L)\,c = -J/D$. Multiply by the integrating factor $e^{zux/L}$ and integrate from $0$ to $L$; the concentrations at the two faces are the bulk values times a partition coefficient $\beta$ that is the same on both sides, so $$J \;=\; P\,zu\,\frac{c_{\text{out}} - c_{\text{in}}e^{zu}}{e^{zu}-1},\qquad P \equiv \frac{D\beta}{L}.$$ This is the constant-field flux equation; $P$ collects everything about the membrane into one number per ion (a permeability, in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the power $P$ of §6 is unrelated). At steady state with no net current, $\sum_i z_iF_{\text{Far}}J_i = 0$. For $z=+1$ the fraction has denominator $e^{u}-1$; for $z=-1$ it has denominator $e^{-u}-1 = -(e^{u}-1)/e^{u}$, and multiplying numerator and denominator by $-e^{u}$ turns the chloride current $zF_{\text{Far}}J_{\mathrm{Cl}}$ into $-F_{\text{Far}}P_{\mathrm{Cl}}\,u\,(c_{\text{out}}e^{u} - c_{\text{in}})/(e^{u}-1)$ — the same form as the cation currents with inside and outside swapped. Every term now shares the factor $u/(e^{u}-1)$, which is nonzero for $u\neq0$ and cancels, leaving $$P_{\mathrm K}\big([\mathrm K]_{\text{out}} - [\mathrm K]_{\text{in}}e^{u}\big) + P_{\mathrm{Na}}\big([\mathrm{Na}]_{\text{out}} - [\mathrm{Na}]_{\text{in}}e^{u}\big) + P_{\mathrm{Cl}}\big([\mathrm{Cl}]_{\text{in}} - [\mathrm{Cl}]_{\text{out}}e^{u}\big) = 0.$$ Solving for $e^{u}$ and taking the logarithm gives the boxed form. Where the hypotheses bind: the field is not in fact uniform across a real membrane, and the ions are not independent (a channel is a pore, not a slab), so $P_i$ is an effective parameter fitted to fluxes rather than a diffusion coefficient; the equation nevertheless reproduces measured resting and peak potentials to a few millivolts, which is why it has survived since 1949. Divalent calcium does not share the common factor and is omitted; its resting permeability is small enough that the omission costs less than a millivolt. ∎

Now the two states of a fibre are two permeability ratios (the plot that follows). At rest potassium and chloride channels dominate: with $P_{\mathrm{Na}}/P_{\mathrm K} = 0.02$ and $P_{\mathrm{Cl}}/P_{\mathrm K} = 2$ (skeletal muscle has an unusually large resting chloride conductance) the lemma gives $V = -86\ \mathrm{mV}$; at $0.01$ it gives $-88.7$ and at $0.05$, $-79.2$. During the spike the voltage-gated sodium channels open and the ratio $P_{\mathrm{Na}}/P_{\mathrm K}$ leaps to about $20$; the same equation then gives $V = +42\ \mathrm{mV}$, the overshoot of a real muscle action potential. Nothing was refitted between the two states: one equation, two assumed permeability ratios, and a $128\ \mathrm{mV}$ swing. Chloride’s role is to hold the resting value near its own Nernst potential and to blunt the overshoot (without it the same ratios give $-80.5$ and $+54\ \mathrm{mV}$), consistent with the clinical fact that loss of the muscle chloride channel produces myotonia, a muscle that cannot stop firing.

Lemma 3.1 drawn for a skeletal-muscle fibre: membrane potential against the sodium-to-potassium permeability ratio, with chloride at twice the potassium permeability (red) and without chloride (dashed blue). The curve runs between the two Nernst potentials of Module 0 (dashed orange). Rest and spike are two points on one curve, $-86$ and $+42\ \mathrm{mV}$.

Every spike moves charge, and the sodium that entered must be pumped back out. Here Module 0’s coupling theorem does the same job it did for calcium. The sodium–potassium pump hydrolyses one ATP to move three $\mathrm{Na^+}$ out and two $\mathrm{K^+}$ in. Take the resting potential as the round measured $-90\ \mathrm{mV}$ rather than the lemma’s $-86$; the $4\ \mathrm{mV}$ moves each electrical term by $0.4\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ and no conclusion below. Its cost is the sum of the electrochemical climbs (Module 0 Definition 5.3): each sodium ion leaving pays the concentration term $R_gT\ln(145/12) = 6.42\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ plus the electrical term of carrying $+1$ charge out against $-90\ \mathrm{mV}$, $F_{\text{Far}}\times0.090\ \mathrm V = 8.68$, together $15.11\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$; each potassium ion entering pays $R_gT\ln(140/4) = 9.17$ but is helped by the field, $-8.68$, net $0.48$. By Module 0 Proposition 3.5 with the pump as the shared intermediate,

$$\Delta G_{\text{net}} \;=\; \Delta G_{\text{ATP}} + 3\,(15.11) + 2\,(0.48) \;=\; -62.5 + 46.3 \;=\; -16.2\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\ \text{at rest},\qquad -6.4\ \text{fatigued},$$

so the three-for-two pump spends $74\%$ of an ATP at rest and $88\%$ at the end of a hard bout. Push the stoichiometry up and the budget runs out: four sodium ions with two potassium cost $61.4\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, permitted at rest by $1.1\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ — inside the uncertainty of the concentrations — and forbidden in a working muscle by $8.7$. Thermodynamics caps the pump at three sodium ions per ATP in the muscle that needs it most, and three is what is observed — the same argument, with the same shape of conclusion, that Module 0 §3 ran for SERCA’s two calcium ions.

How much does excitability cost, then, against the contraction it triggers? Charging a membrane capacitance $C_m$ through the spike’s swing $\Delta V$ moves a charge $C_m\Delta V$ per unit area — for a cylinder of radius $r$ that is $2C_m\Delta V/(rF_{\text{Far}})$ moles per unit volume — and every coulomb of it is sodium the pump must return. With $C_m\approx5\ \mu\mathrm{F\,cm^{-2}}$ of fibre surface (the T-tubules of Fig. 9 multiply the bare bilayer’s $1\ \mu\mathrm{F\,cm^{-2}}$), $\Delta V = 130\ \mathrm{mV}$ and $r = 25\ \mu\mathrm m$, that is $5.4\ \mu\mathrm M$ of sodium per impulse, costing $1.8\ \mu\mathrm M$ of ATP at three per ATP. Set that beside the contraction: the fibre holds about $90\ \mu\mathrm M$ of myosin heads (the $6.0\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{m^{-2}}$ filaments of Lemma 2.1, $294$ heads each, per $2.7\ \mu\mathrm m$ of sarcomere, times the myofibril fraction $\chi = 0.83$), and each spends an ATP per cycle. If every head cycled once, the electrical signal would cost about $2\%$ of the mechanical bill. The nervous system’s command is nearly free; what costs is the work it orders and the calcium it must then put away.

Calcium unblocks the sites — and defines activation

Now the payoff. In a resting fibre the actin binding sites are masked by tropomyosin, a long strand lying along the thin filament, held in its blocking position by the three-part troponin complex. No calcium, no attachment, no force. When Ca²⁺ rises, it binds the troponin, which swivels and drags the tropomyosin down into the groove of the actin helix — uncovering the sites so the crossbridges of §2 can grab on and cycle (Fig. 10):

Definition 3.1 (activation). The activation $a$ is the fraction of actin binding sites made available — equivalently, the fraction of the crossbridge machinery switched on — ranging from $a=0$ (fully blocked, relaxed) to $a=1$ (all sites exposed, maximal). It is the factor that scales the crossbridge count of §2, and it enters the muscle force as $$F_{\text{active}} = a\,f_L(\ell)\,f_V(v)\,F_{\max}.$$ (Symbol note: this activation $a$ is unrelated to the thin-filament length $a_{\text{thin}}$ of §2, which always carries its subscript.)

How does $a$ depend on the calcium level? Each troponin binds more than one Ca²⁺, and neighbouring troponin–tropomyosin units cooperate — once one lets go of the tropomyosin, its neighbours follow. That cooperativity makes the site-availability a steep, switch-like function of calcium, well captured by a Hill relation:

Proposition 3.1 (steady-state activation). Under a fixed (clamped) calcium level, the equilibrium fraction of exposed sites is $$a_\infty([\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}]) \;=\; \frac{[\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}]^{\,n}}{Ca_{50}^{\,n} + [\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}]^{\,n}},$$ with cooperativity (Hill) exponent $n\approx2$–$4$ and half-activation $Ca_{50}\approx0.5$–$1\ \mu\mathrm M$. It is $\approx0$ at the resting $0.1\ \mu\mathrm M$ and saturates toward $1$ well above $Ca_{50}$ (plotted in Fig. 11).
Take the smallest setting that shows the mechanism: all-or-none cooperativity, in which a troponin–tropomyosin unit binds either no calcium or all $n$ ions at once. Write $T$ for a blocked unit and $T\!\cdot\!\mathrm{Ca}_n$ for an unblocked one. The single reaction is $$T+n\,\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\ ⇌\ T\!\cdot\!\mathrm{Ca}_n,\qquad K_d=\frac{[T]\,[\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}]^{\,n}}{[T\!\cdot\!\mathrm{Ca}_n]}.$$ The exposed fraction is $a_\infty=[T\!\cdot\!\mathrm{Ca}_n]/([T]+[T\!\cdot\!\mathrm{Ca}_n])$. Divide numerator and denominator by $[T]$ and substitute $[T\!\cdot\!\mathrm{Ca}_n]/[T]=[\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}]^{\,n}/K_d$: $$a_\infty=\frac{[\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}]^{\,n}/K_d}{1+[\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}]^{\,n}/K_d}=\frac{[\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}]^{\,n}}{K_d+[\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}]^{\,n}},$$ which is the stated form with $Ca_{50}=K_d^{1/n}$: at $[\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}]=Ca_{50}$ the two terms are equal and $a_\infty=\tfrac12$. Where the hypothesis binds: real binding is graded, not all-or-none, so the fitted $n$ is an apparent cooperativity that need not be a whole number, and $n\approx2$–$4$ against three or four physical sites is the price of the approximation. In the limit of no cooperativity ($n=1$) the expression collapses to the ordinary saturating isotherm $[\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}]/(K_d+[\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}])$, which rises far too gently to work as a switch. ∎

The single twitch

The sigmoid is the steady-state answer — where activation settles under a held calcium level. But a single nerve impulse gives only a brief calcium spike, and the thin filament cannot follow it instantly: binding calcium and sliding tropomyosin take time. So activation relaxes toward its steady-state target with a time constant $\tau_a$, $$\frac{da}{dt} = \frac{a_\infty\!\big([\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}](t)\big) - a}{\tau_a},$$

Modelling assumption 3.2 (the calcium pulse and its constants). One impulse releases a calcium pulse whose normalised shape is the difference of a fast release and a slow re-uptake, the two processes drawn in Fig. 9: $$p(t)=\frac{1}{p_{\max}}\Big(1-e^{-t/\tau_r}\Big)e^{-t/\tau_d},\qquad t\ge 0,$$ with a release constant $\tau_r=3.6\ \mathrm{ms}$ (RyR opening) and a re-uptake constant $\tau_d=18\ \mathrm{ms}$ (SERCA pumping); $p_{\max}$ normalises the peak to $1$, which the shape reaches at $t=\tau_r\ln(1+\tau_d/\tau_r)=6.4\ \mathrm{ms}$. The free calcium is then $[\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}](t)=\mathrm{Ca}_{\text{rest}}+(\mathrm{Ca}_{\text{peak}}-\mathrm{Ca}_{\text{rest}})\,p(t)$ with $\mathrm{Ca}_{\text{rest}}=0.1\ \mu\mathrm M$ and $\mathrm{Ca}_{\text{peak}}=1.4\ \mu\mathrm M$, and the activation follows the relaxation above with $\tau_a=41\ \mathrm{ms}$. These four constants are assumed, chosen so the twitch matches the measured fast-fibre features quoted below; K10 estimates $\tau_a$ from those features instead. Every computed number in this section and in §4 comes from integrating this model, and the code is in K2's solution.

measured, not derived: the release constant $\tau_r = 3.6\ \mathrm{ms}$ and the re-uptake constant $\tau_d = 18\ \mathrm{ms}$ are chosen to reproduce measured calcium transients, and nothing in this course predicts them. What would: $\tau_r$ is the open-time kinetics of the RyR channel, and $\tau_d$ is the ratio of the calcium load to the SERCA pumping rate — a saturable enzyme rate of the kind Module 0 §6 derives (its Proposition 6.4), which would need the pump density and the turnover number per pump as inputs. Both are measured quantities this module does not carry, so the two constants stay assumed, and K10 shows how much of a fitted $\tau_a$ they silently absorb.

The relaxation above is exactly the activation dynamics §5 will formalise (there, driven directly by the neural command). Chaining calcium→$a_\infty$→$a$ and remembering that force tracks $a$ (force $\propto a$), one action potential produces a single twitch (Fig. 12):

Validation. The computed twitch has a peak activation $a=0.22$, a time-to-peak of $24.8$ ms and a half-relaxation of $38.1$ ms (Modelling assumption 3.2 integrated; the code is in K2's solution) — squarely in the measured range for a fast (type II) fibre (time-to-peak ${\sim}20$–$40$ ms); slow (type I) fibres are two to three times slower, a fibre-type spread that §4 puts to use. The delay of a few milliseconds between the impulse and the first rise of force is the electromechanical delay measured in the lab.

The single twitch is the atom of muscle force, but by itself it is feeble — a fifth of the way to full activation, and already fading before it peaks. The gap between one twitch and that tetanic ceiling is the entire opportunity the nervous system exploits: fire the impulses fast enough and the twitches pile on top of one another, summing toward a fused, maximal contraction. Cashing that in — twitch summation, motor-unit recruitment, and the fibre types just mentioned — is §4.

4. Motor units, recruitment, and rate coding

§3 left us with a feeble atom. One nerve impulse releases one calcium pulse, which drives activation up to only $a\approx0.22$ — under a third of the tetanic ceiling $a_\infty\approx0.73$ — and the twitch is already fading before it peaks (Fig. 12). Yet a whole muscle grades its force smoothly from the whisper that threads a needle to the surge that lifts a barbell. Between the feeble twitch and that range lies the nervous system’s control problem, and it has exactly two knobs to turn:

  • Recruitment — how many motor units it switches on, and
  • Rate coding — how fast it fires each one.

This section builds both, then collapses them into a single lumped command $u(t)\in[0,1]$ — the neural drive, or excitation, that §5 turns into the activation $a$ the force laws multiply. We start with the quantum the whole scheme is built from.

The motor unit: the quantum of contraction

A muscle fibre never fires alone. Its command arrives down an α-motoneuron — a nerve cell whose body sits in the spinal cord and whose single axon runs out to the muscle, there branching to contact many fibres. Every fibre it touches is wired to that one neuron and no other (Fig. 13):

Definition 4.1 (motor unit). A motor unit is one α-motoneuron together with all the muscle fibres it innervates. It is all-or-none: when the motoneuron fires an action potential, every fibre in the unit is excited and twitches together. The motor unit — not the single fibre — is therefore the smallest packet of force the nervous system can command. You cannot fire half a motor unit.

A muscle is a pool of many motor units sharing the tissue, and their fibres are interdigitated rather than clumped: the fibres of any one unit are scattered through the whole cross-section, so its contraction pulls evenly on the whole muscle rather than tugging one corner. Switching a unit on adds its fibres’ force to the total; that is the physical act of recruitment.

Motor units come in a graded range of sizes

Units are not identical — they span a wide, orderly range, and this is the fibre-type spread §3 flagged when the twitch turned out to be a fast-fibre twitch. Three broad classes span the range:

TypeFibres per unitTwitchFatigueRole
S — slow (type I)few (tens–hundreds)small, slowvery resistantposture, all-day work
FR — fast, resistant (IIa)intermediatemedium, fastresistantsustained locomotion
FF — fast, fatigable (IIx)many (up to thousands)large, fastfatigues quicklybursts, maximal effort

The slow twitch of type I fibres is two to three times slower than the fast twitch we computed in §3; the force a unit can add ranges over roughly two orders of magnitude from the smallest S unit to the largest FF unit. That huge span is exactly what makes the order of recruitment matter.

Henneman’s size principle: recruitment order is set by biophysics

Motor units are recruited in a fixed order — smallest first, largest last — regardless of the movement. This is the size principle (Henneman, 1957), and the nervous system does not have to arrange it: the order falls straight out of a one-line circuit argument (Fig. 14, inset).

A motoneuron fires when a descending synaptic current $I$ charges its cell membrane past a voltage threshold. Model the membrane as a resistance $R$ — its input resistance, the voltage change produced per unit injected current. A small motoneuron has little membrane area, hence a high input resistance; a large one has more membrane and a lower resistance. By Ohm’s law the depolarisation a shared drive current produces is

$$\Delta V \;=\; I\,R,\qquad R_{\text{small}} \gg R_{\text{large}} \;\Longrightarrow\; \Delta V_{\text{small}} \gg \Delta V_{\text{large}}.$$

The same command current depolarises the high-resistance small neuron the most, so it reaches threshold first; as the command grows, progressively larger (lower-resistance) neurons cross threshold in turn. Recruitment order is not a control decision — it is forced by cell size. The consequence is a beautifully useful one (Fig. 14):

Because the small units recruited first add little force and the large units recruited last add a great deal, force is built in fine increments at low effort and coarse ones near maximum. You get your most delicate force control exactly where daily life needs it, and the fatigue-resistant S units carry the continuous postural load while the fatigable FF reserve waits for emergencies. Fine motor resolution follows from $\Delta V = IR$ alone.

Rate coding: firing faster sums the twitches

Recruitment sets how many units are on; the second knob grades the force of each unit already recruited by changing its firing rate — how many impulses per second it fires. This works because of the timescale mismatch §3 built in: the twitch outlasts the impulse that caused it. Activation peaks near $25$ ms and is still relaxing at $40$ ms and beyond, but a motoneuron can fire again far sooner. Fire the next impulse before the last twitch has relaxed and its calcium re-opens the gate while activation is still elevated — so the twitches sum.

We can compute this exactly, and consistently with §3, because the machinery is already in hand. Each impulse fires the same calcium pulse of §3. Calcium release saturates — a fibre cannot dump more than the sarcoplasmic reticulum holds — so the calcium from a train is not a runaway sum but a saturating combination of single pulses,

$$[\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}](t) \;=\; \mathrm{Ca}_{\text{rest}} + \big(\mathrm{Ca}_{\text{peak}}-\mathrm{Ca}_{\text{rest}}\big)\Big(1-\prod_i \big[1-p(t-t_i)\big]\Big),$$

where $p$ is the normalised single-pulse shape of §3 and the $t_i$ are the impulse times. For one impulse this reduces to §3’s twitch exactly; for a fast train it saturates at the single-pulse peak $1.4\ \mu\mathrm M$, so the steady-state target $a_\infty([\mathrm{Ca}])$ is pinned at $0.73$ and can never exceed it. Feed this calcium into §3’s activation equation $\dot a=(a_\infty-a)/\tau_a$ with the same $\tau_a\approx41$ ms and integrate. The result is the whole story of graded force in one figure (Fig. 15):

Three regimes emerge as the firing rate climbs. At $10$ Hz the impulses fall more than a twitch-width apart, so activation partly relaxes between them: force is a bumpy, unfused tetanus (mean $\bar a\approx0.15$), the individual twitches still visible as ripples. At $25$ Hz the ripple shrinks and the mean climbs to $\bar a\approx0.38$. By $60$ Hz the impulses come so fast that activation has no time to fall between them: the ripple vanishes and force settles onto a smooth fused tetanus at $\bar a\approx0.69$, essentially the $0.73$ that sustained calcium would give. The point to hold onto is where the summation lives — not in the calcium, which merely saturates, but in the slow variable $a$, which climbs because each impulse arrives before it has had time to relax. That build-up is easier to follow in motion (Fig. 16):

Fusion frequency and the force–frequency curve

How fast is “fast enough”? The ripple disappears once the interval between impulses drops below the twitch’s own contraction time — its time-to-peak, ${\approx}25$ ms — so that a fresh impulse lands before activation has begun to fall. Sweeping the rate and measuring both the mean force and the residual ripple gives the muscle’s force–frequency curve (Fig. 17):

Force rises steeply with rate, then saturates: once firing is fast enough to fuse, adding rate buys almost nothing, because $a$ is already pinned at its ceiling. The ripple collapses to nothing by the fusion frequency $f_{\text{fus}}\approx42$ Hz — the rate above which the peak-to-trough ripple stays under $5\%$, put at $42.5$ Hz by the sweep of K2 — which sits right at $1/(\text{contraction time})\approx1/(25\ \mathrm{ms})=40$ Hz, as it must: fusion is exactly the rate at which the next impulse arrives by the time the twitch peaks. Below $f_{\text{fus}}$ force ripples and rate coding is the CNS’s fine dial; above it, only recruiting more units adds meaningful force. Fast (type II) fibres, with their briefer twitches, fuse at higher rates than slow (type I) fibres — the same fibre-type spread, seen from the frequency side.

Neural drive: one command for both knobs

Recruitment and rate coding are not independent. As effort rises the two climb together: new units switch on while the units already on fire faster. Because a Hill-type muscle model does not track individual motoneurons, we do not need them separately — we need the single aggregate command they produce. That is the neural drive (Fig. 18):

Definition 4.2 (neural drive / excitation). The neural drive $u(t)\in[0,1]$ is the normalised, whole-muscle excitation that aggregates recruitment and rate coding into one lumped command: $u=0$ is a silent muscle, $u=1$ is every motor unit recruited and firing fast enough to fuse. It is a dimensionless input, not yet a force — the CNS’s single knob on the muscle.

Framing $u$ as a single number is the modelling choice that makes the next step tractable: it is the input to the activation dynamics. But $u$ is a command, and the muscle cannot obey it instantly — binding and clearing calcium and cycling crossbridges all take time, the same lag $\tau_a$ that made a single twitch peak $25$ ms after its impulse. §5 makes that precise, turning $u$ into activation $a$ through a single first-order ODE — the same equation we have already been integrating in miniature — with asymmetric rise and fall times that explain why force both lags the command and outlasts it.

5. Activation dynamics: turning the command into activation

§4 compressed the whole nervous-system side of the problem into one number, the neural drive $u(t)\in[0,1]$. But $u$ is a command, not a force — and §0 warned that a muscle does not obey a command the instant it arrives. Decide to lift and the force ramps up over a fraction of a second; let go and it lingers. This section writes down the dynamics behind that lag: the rule that turns the command $u$ into the activation $a$ the force laws multiply.

The activation ODE

The shape of the answer is already in hand. In §3 activation chased a calcium-set target $a_\infty$ by first-order relaxation, $\dot a=(a_\infty-a)/\tau_a$. §4 then showed that what sets the calcium level, muscle-wide, is the drive $u$: more recruitment and faster firing raise calcium, and so raise the target. Collapsing that chain — command $\to$ calcium $\to$ target — lets us drive the activation with $u$ itself. Activation relaxes toward the command:

$$\dot a \;=\; \frac{u - a}{\tau_a},\qquad a,\,u\in[0,1].$$

Read it plainly: whenever the command $u$ sits above the current activation $a$ the muscle switches on ($\dot a\gt 0$); when $u$ falls below $a$ it switches off. The parameter $\tau_a$ is a time constant — the time to close the fraction $1-1/e\approx63\%$ of the gap between $a$ and $u$; a small $\tau_a$ means a brisk response, a large one a sluggish one. This first-order relaxation is the "activation dynamics" the model has been promising since §0. One thing about it is still too crude, though: it uses the same $\tau_a$ whether the muscle is switching on or off — and those are not equally fast.

Rise is faster than fall: two time constants

Turning a muscle on is quicker than letting it relax. So the honest model carries two time constants, and picks whichever applies to the direction the activation is currently moving:

Definition 5.1 (activation and deactivation time constants). The activation time constant $\tau_{\text{act}}$ governs how fast $a$ rises toward a larger command; the deactivation time constant $\tau_{\text{deact}}$ governs how fast it falls toward a smaller one. In skeletal muscle rise is faster than fall, $\tau_{\text{act}}\approx10\ \mathrm{ms}\lt \tau_{\text{deact}}\approx40\ \mathrm{ms}$.

With the constant chosen by direction, the activation ODE becomes the form used throughout the rest of the module — its boxed activation law, standing beside the length–tension law of §2:

$$\boxed{\;\dot a \;=\; \frac{u-a}{\tau_a(u,a)},\qquad \tau_a(u,a)=\begin{cases}\tau_{\text{act}}, & u\gt a\quad(\text{switching on}),\\[2pt]\tau_{\text{deact}}, & u\le a\quad(\text{switching off}).\end{cases}\;}$$

This also settles a loose thread. §3 and §4 integrated the same first-order equation with a single $\tau_a\approx41\ \mathrm{ms}$ — which we can now name: that was the deactivation constant, calibrated to the slow relaxing tail of the twitch. Splitting it lets the on-transition run at its own, faster $\tau_{\text{act}}$, which is why real force rises more briskly than a single-time-constant twitch would suggest. The consequences are cleanest to see in the response to a simple on/off command (Fig. 19):

The two constants can be read straight off the curve. After the command switches on, activation covers $63\%$ of its climb in one $\tau_{\text{act}}\approx10\ \mathrm{ms}$; after it switches off, activation still retains $37\%$ a full $\tau_{\text{deact}}\approx40\ \mathrm{ms}$ later. Between the command and the first stirrings of force sits a few-millisecond electromechanical delay — the same lag §3 measured in the twitch. Both features of §0’s list are now accounted for: force lags the command switching on and outlasts it switching off.

Why the asymmetry — calcium in fast, out slow

The rise-fall asymmetry is not fitted; it falls out of how a fibre moves calcium, the machinery of §3 (Fig. 20):

Calcium enters the cytosol the fast way — by opening a channel, the RyR, which lets it pour down its concentration gradient the instant the action potential arrives. It can leave only the slow way — by being pumped back into the store against that gradient, one ATP burned per two ions, by SERCA. Opening a gate is quicker than bailing the room dry, so activation climbs with the small $\tau_{\text{act}}$ and ebbs with the larger $\tau_{\text{deact}}$. The asymmetry is a direct fingerprint of the release-then-reuptake calcium transient drawn in §3.

Where the two time constants come from: the kinetics of the calcium switch

Fig. 20 gives the asymmetry a mechanism in words: a channel opens fast, a pump bails slowly. That is the right picture for the calcium, but $\tau_{\text{act}}$ and $\tau_{\text{deact}}$ are constants of the activation, and activation is the calcium bound to troponin. So the question is what the binding step itself contributes, and Module 0 §6 supplies the tool: mass action (its Definition 6.1), under which a binding reaction has a forward rate proportional to the reactant concentrations and a backward rate proportional to the bound complex, with rate constant $k_{\text{off}}$. Apply it to the all-or-none troponin unit that the proof of Proposition 3.1 used. (Module 0 writes the Hill exponent $n_H$; this module keeps its own $n$.)

Proposition 5.1 (the kinetic origin of the activation time constants). Let the troponin–tropomyosin unit bind $n$ calcium ions all-or-none with an $n$-th-order on-rate constant $k^{(n)}_{\text{on}}$ and an off-rate constant $k_{\text{off}}$, at a free calcium concentration $[\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}]$ that is held fixed. Then the exposed fraction $a$ obeys $$\frac{\mathrm da}{\mathrm dt} \;=\; k^{(n)}_{\text{on}}[\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}]^{\,n}\,(1-a) - k_{\text{off}}\,a \;=\; \frac{a_\infty - a}{\tau(\mathrm{Ca})},$$ a first-order relaxation toward the steady state $a_\infty$ of Proposition 3.1 with $Ca_{50}^{\,n} = k_{\text{off}}/k^{(n)}_{\text{on}}$, and with a time constant that depends on the calcium level: $$\boxed{\;\tau(\mathrm{Ca}) \;=\; \frac{1}{k^{(n)}_{\text{on}}[\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}]^{\,n} + k_{\text{off}}} \;=\; \frac{\tau_{\text{deact}}}{1 + \big([\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}]/Ca_{50}\big)^{n}},\qquad \tau_{\text{deact}} \equiv \frac{1}{k_{\text{off}}}\;}$$ Switching off happens at resting calcium, where the on-term is negligible, so the deactivation constant is the unbinding time alone. Switching on happens at elevated calcium, where both terms act, so $\tau_{\text{act}}$ is shorter than $\tau_{\text{deact}}$ by the factor $1+([\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}]/Ca_{50})^{n}$. The asymmetry of Definition 5.1 is structural, not fitted.
With $[\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}]$ fixed, mass action for the single reaction $T + n\,\mathrm{Ca}^{2+} \rightleftharpoons T\!\cdot\!\mathrm{Ca}_n$ of Proposition 3.1’s proof gives a forward rate $k^{(n)}_{\text{on}}[\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}]^{\,n}$ per blocked unit and a backward rate $k_{\text{off}}$ per unblocked one. If $a$ is the unblocked fraction, blocked units are $1-a$, and the net rate of unblocking is the first expression. It is linear in $a$: collect terms as $\mathrm da/\mathrm dt = -\big(k^{(n)}_{\text{on}}[\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}]^{\,n} + k_{\text{off}}\big)\,a + k^{(n)}_{\text{on}}[\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}]^{\,n}$, which is $(a_\infty - a)/\tau$ with $1/\tau$ the coefficient of $-a$ and $a_\infty = k^{(n)}_{\text{on}}[\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}]^{\,n}\,\tau$. Substituting $\tau$ gives $a_\infty = [\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}]^{\,n}/\big([\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}]^{\,n} + k_{\text{off}}/k^{(n)}_{\text{on}}\big)$, which is Proposition 3.1’s form once $Ca_{50}^{\,n}$ is identified with $k_{\text{off}}/k^{(n)}_{\text{on}}$ — the same identification Module 0 Proposition 6.1 makes for a single site, that an equilibrium constant is a ratio of two rates. Factoring $k_{\text{off}}$ out of $1/\tau$ gives the second boxed form. At $[\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}] \ll Ca_{50}$, $\tau \to 1/k_{\text{off}}$; at $[\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}] \gg Ca_{50}$, $\tau \to 0$ as $[\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}]^{-n}$. Where the hypotheses bind: calcium is held fixed, so this is the relaxation at a clamped level, and a real twitch, in which calcium itself rises and falls, must be integrated (K11); and the all-or-none unit is the idealisation Proposition 3.1 already named, so the constants are apparent ones — Module 0 §6 shows why a Hill exponent is a fitted steepness rather than a molecular count. ∎

Now the numbers, and they are not new inputs. Definition 5.1’s $\tau_{\text{deact}} \approx 40\ \mathrm{ms}$ fixes $k_{\text{off}} = 25\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$; Proposition 3.1’s $Ca_{50} = 1\ \mu\mathrm M$ and $n = 3$ then fix $k^{(3)}_{\text{on}} = k_{\text{off}}/Ca_{50}^{3} = 25\ \mu\mathrm{M^{-3}\,s^{-1}}$. At the twitch’s calcium peak of $1.4\ \mu\mathrm M$ (Modelling assumption 3.2) the on-term is $25\times1.4^{3} = 68.6\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$, so

$$\tau_{\text{act}} \;=\; \frac{40\ \mathrm{ms}}{1 + (1.4/1)^{3}} \;=\; \frac{40}{3.74} \;=\; 10.7\ \mathrm{ms},$$

against the $\approx10\ \mathrm{ms}$ Definition 5.1 quoted from measurement. The ratio of four between the two constants is the number $1 + 1.4^{3}$, and it came from the calcium switch’s own steepness and the height of one twitch’s calcium pulse (the plot below). Two checks say the picture is consistent rather than merely arranged. Module 0 §6 quotes a measured per-site association rate for calcium onto its binding proteins of $k_{\text{on}} \approx 10^{8}\ \mathrm{M^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$, a few per cent of the diffusion limit; at $Ca_{50} = 1\ \mu\mathrm M$ that is $100\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ per site, a $10\ \mathrm{ms}$ binding time — the same order as $\tau_{\text{act}}$, though it is a different constant (a per-site rate in $\mathrm{M^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$, not the $n$-th-order rate of the all-or-none unit) and is a consistency check, not a derivation. And $k_{\text{off}} = 25\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ is four times below the $100\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ Module 0 quotes for the isolated protein, a gap that Module 0’s stated factor of two to three plus the filament’s cooperativity covers only marginally — it is an apparent constant of the all-or-none unit, consistent with Module 0 §6’s note that a site’s rates on the filament are not the isolated protein’s, and not a check.

Proposition 5.1’s time constant against free calcium, on a log axis, for $k_{\text{off}} = 25\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $Ca_{50} = 1\ \mu\mathrm M$, $n = 3$. At resting calcium it is the unbinding time, $40\ \mathrm{ms}$; at the twitch peak it has fallen to $10.7\ \mathrm{ms}$. The two constants of Definition 5.1 are two points on one curve.

derived here: $\tau_{\text{act}} = 10.7\ \mathrm{ms}$ follows from Proposition 5.1 with three inputs the module already carried — the deactivation constant, the half-activation level and the Hill exponent — plus the twitch’s peak calcium. No new measurement enters. What it inherits is the status of those inputs: $Ca_{50}$ and $n$ are fitted steepnesses (Module 0 §6), and the calcium peak is assumed (Modelling assumption 3.2), so the $10.7$ is only as good as the $1.4\ \mu\mathrm M$: at a $2\ \mu\mathrm M$ peak the same formula gives $4.4\ \mathrm{ms}$.

measured, not derived: $\tau_{\text{deact}} \approx 40\ \mathrm{ms}$ is the unbinding time of calcium from troponin, $1/k_{\text{off}}$, and Module 0 §6 is explicit that association and dissociation rate constants come from stopped-flow and temperature-jump kinetics (rapid-mixing and rapid-heating experiments that time a single binding step) and are predicted by nothing in this course. Proposition 5.1 explains why the ratio of the two constants is what it is; it takes one of them from measurement.

measured, not derived: the rate constants of the switch, $k_{\text{off}} = 25\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $k^{(3)}_{\text{on}} = 25\ \mu\mathrm{M^{-3}\,s^{-1}}$, are not new inputs but the measured $\tau_{\text{deact}}$ and the fitted $Ca_{50}$ rewritten as rates through $k_{\text{off}} = 1/\tau_{\text{deact}}$ and $k^{(3)}_{\text{on}} = k_{\text{off}}/Ca_{50}^{3}$; they inherit both provenances, and the $n$-th-order on-rate in particular is an apparent constant of the all-or-none idealisation, not a per-site rate that a stopped-flow experiment reports.

One thing this does not explain, and it is worth saying before K11 finds it. Proposition 5.1 makes the calcium switch fast at high calcium — faster than the twitch of Fig. 12 rises. Integrate its kinetics through the assumed calcium pulse and the activation peaks near $18\ \mathrm{ms}$ at $k_{\text{off}} = 25\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ (K11 puts it at $18.7$ for the off-rate that matches the tail), not the measured $25$; binding cannot be slowed to fix that without lengthening the tail, which the measured half-relaxation forbids. The missing $6$–$7\ \mathrm{ms}$ must live downstream of binding — in tropomyosin’s movement and the crossbridges’ own attachment, which the single state $a$ of Definition 3.1 lumps together. K11 makes the argument quantitative, and finds that the twitch alone cannot say where the slowness lives.

Activation is a low-pass filter of the drive

A muscle almost never receives a clean on/off step; the drive rises and falls gradually as effort is graded through a movement. The activation ODE then acts as a low-pass filter — a smoother that passes slow changes in the command and blurs fast ones (Fig. 21):

Two things follow, and both matter downstream. First, activation cannot answer arbitrarily fast: rapid flickers in drive are smoothed away, so a muscle is a sluggish transducer of intent. Second, because deactivation is the slower leg, force always outlives its command — when $u$ has returned to zero the activation is still more than half-on. This lingering activation is exactly what a movement controller must anticipate, and it is the reason a Hill-type model needs a state ($a$) with memory rather than an instantaneous input.

With activation dynamics in hand we hold three of the four factors that scale muscle force: the maximal force $F_{\max}$ of §1, the length factor $f_L$ of §2, and now the activation $a$ that §3–§5 built from a nerve impulse. Only the velocity factor $f_V$ remains: force also depends on how fast the muscle is shortening, because the crossbridge cycle of §2 takes time. That is §6, and with it the model is ready to assemble.

6. The force–velocity relation: Hill’s hyperbola

§2 found how force depends on the muscle’s length. But a muscle in a movement is rarely holding still — it is shortening or being stretched, and its force depends just as strongly on how fast. Everyone has felt it: a light dumbbell flies up, a heavy one crawls; and lowering a weight you cannot possibly lift is easy. Those are the two halves of the force–velocity relation, the third factor $f_V$ in the force product $F_{\text{active}}=a\,f_L\,f_V\,F_{\max}$.

Shortening weakens, lengthening strengthens

Fix the sign convention first. Let $v$ be the shortening velocity — the rate at which the muscle’s length decreases. Then $v\gt0$ is concentric action (the muscle shortens while pulling, as in lifting), $v=0$ is isometric (fixed length, the holding case of §2), and $v\lt0$ is eccentric action (the muscle is forcibly lengthened while resisting, as in lowering). Measuring force at each velocity traces one curve (Fig. 22):

On the shortening side the force follows a hyperbola that A. V. Hill fitted in 1938 from heat-and-work measurements on frog muscle:

Proposition 6.1 (Hill’s force–velocity equation, 1938). During concentric shortening the tension $F$ and shortening velocity $v$ satisfy $$\big(F+a_H\big)\big(v+b_H\big)=\big(F_0+a_H\big)\,b_H,$$ a rectangular hyperbola with two constants: $a_H$ (units of force) and $b_H$ (units of velocity). $F_0$ is the isometric force ($v=0$), and the curve crosses zero force at the maximum shortening velocity $v_{\max}=b_H F_0/a_H$, beyond which the muscle cannot shorten fast enough to bear any load. The ratio $a_H/F_0\approx0.25$ sets the curvature.
The hyperbola is not a curve fit; it follows in two lines from the two measurements Hill made. (i) Shortening heat. A muscle shortening by $\Delta x$ liberates extra heat $a_H\,\Delta x$ beyond its isometric rate, so the extra heat rate is $a_H v$; the constant $a_H$ has units of force because heat per unit length is a force. (ii) Energy-rate law. The total extra energy rate, heat plus mechanical work, falls linearly to zero as the load approaches the isometric force: $$\underbrace{F v}_{\text{work rate}}+\underbrace{a_H v}_{\text{shortening heat rate}}=b_H\,(F_0-F),$$ with $b_H$ the constant of proportionality, a velocity. That is the whole content of the measurement. Now add $b_H\,(F+a_H)$ to both sides: $$(F+a_H)\,v+b_H\,(F+a_H)=b_H\,(F_0-F)+b_H\,(F+a_H)=b_H\,(F_0+a_H),$$ and the left side factors, giving $(F+a_H)(v+b_H)=(F_0+a_H)\,b_H$. Where the hypotheses bind: (ii) is a statement about steady shortening at a fixed activation and length, so the hyperbola is a steady-state law and says nothing about the transient after a load step. At $v=0$ it returns $F=F_0$, as it must; the two constants are what a heat-and-work experiment measures, not free parameters fitted to the force curve itself. ∎

Solving for force and normalising by $F_0$ gives the dimensionless velocity factor $f_V=F/F_0$ the model uses — the second mechanical law of the module, after the length–tension law of §2:

$$\boxed{\;f_V(v)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1-v/v_{\max}}{1+v/(c\,v_{\max})}, & v\ge0\quad(\text{concentric, Hill}),\\[10pt] 1+(f_{\text{ecc}}-1)\dfrac{k\,(-v)}{v_{\max}+k\,(-v)}, & v\lt0\quad(\text{eccentric}),\end{cases}\;}$$

with curvature $c=a_H/F_0\approx0.25$ and an eccentric plateau $f_{\text{ecc}}\approx1.5$.
