The concentric branch falls from $f_V=1$ at isometric to $0$ at $v_{\max}$; the eccentric branch rises above $1$, levelling near $1.5\,F_0$. The join at $v=0$ is a kink, not a smooth peak, and the shape constant $k$ is what fixes how sharp it is. Differentiate each branch at $v=0$: the concentric slope is $-(1+1/c)/v_{\max}$ and the eccentric slope is $-(f_{\text{ecc}}-1)k/v_{\max}$. Requiring the eccentric branch to climb twice as steeply as the concentric branch falls gives $$k=\frac{2\,(1+1/c)}{f_{\text{ecc}}-1}=\frac{2\,(1+4)}{0.5}=20,$$ the value every eccentric curve in this module and the labs of §9 use. So a muscle gives up force reluctantly as it shortens but gains it readily as it is stretched.

Why speed costs force: the crossbridges take time

Both halves of the curve come straight from the crossbridge cycle of §2, where force is proportional to the number of heads attached at any instant. A head needs time to attach, drive its power stroke, and release (Fig. 23):

When the filaments slide slowly, nearly every head is attached and pulling, so force is close to $F_0$. As shortening speeds up, each head is dragged past its working range before it can complete a stroke and reattach, so fewer are attached at any moment and force falls — until, at $v_{\max}$, cycling cannot keep up at all and net force vanishes. This also ties $v_{\max}$ back to §2: a fibre’s top speed is set by how fast its crossbridges cycle, which is exactly what makes fast (type II) fibres fast. The eccentric rise is the same mechanism run backwards: a head that is forcibly stretched while attached bears more tension than it generates on its own, and lengthening pops attached heads loose so that fresh ones re-engage under strain — so eccentric force exceeds $F_0$, at a fraction of the metabolic cost.

Why a cold muscle is slow: $v_{\max}$ as a rate

The last paragraph made $v_{\max}$ a rate in disguise: a fibre’s top speed is set by how fast its crossbridges can cycle. Make that explicit. At $v_{\max}$ a head that has just completed its stroke of $d = 10\ \mathrm{nm}$ must detach before the sliding drags it into a position where it resists; if the rate-limiting step of the cycle runs at $k_{\text{cyc}}$ per second, each half-sarcomere can shorten at most about $d\,k_{\text{cyc}}$ per second, and a fibre of $N_{\text{hs}}$ half-sarcomeres in series at $N_{\text{hs}}\,d\,k_{\text{cyc}}$. (The symbol $k_{\text{cyc}}$ is a rate constant; it is not the eccentric shape constant $k = 20$ of the box above.) Run the picture backwards on the fast-fibre $v_{\max} = 8\,\ell_0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ that the labs of §7 and §9 use (the upper half of the Appendix’s $5$–$10$ range): at eight optimal lengths per second each half-sarcomere of $1.35\ \mu\mathrm m$ shortens at $10.8\ \mu\mathrm m\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, which demands $k_{\text{cyc}} \approx 1080\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$. That is the order of the ATP-induced detachment rate that solution kinetics measures for fast myosin, so the picture is self-consistent — though a rate inferred from $v_{\max}$ cannot then be used to predict $v_{\max}$.

This is a hundred times the $\approx10\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ per-head ATP turnover that Module 0 §6 uses for its barrier check. The two are different quantities — the turnover of the whole cycle by a head that spends most of its time detached, against the detachment step alone — and the detachment step is taken to share the cycle’s measured $Q_{10}$, which is what lets Proposition 6.2 borrow Module 0’s barrier for the step that limits speed.

What the rate picture does predict is what happens when the temperature changes, because a rate constant carries a barrier, and Module 0 §6 has already computed the barrier for this cycle.

Proposition 6.2 (the temperature scaling of the force–velocity curve). Let the maximum shortening velocity be proportional to a single rate-limiting step of the crossbridge cycle, $v_{\max} \propto k_{\text{cyc}}(T)$, with $k_{\text{cyc}}$ obeying the Arrhenius law of Module 0 Proposition 6.3 with activation energy $E_a$; and let the isometric force $F_0$ and the curvature $c$ be independent of temperature. Then between absolute temperatures $T_0$ and $T$ $$\boxed{\;\frac{v_{\max}(T)}{v_{\max}(T_0)} \;=\; \exp\!\left[-\frac{E_a}{R_g}\left(\frac1T - \frac1{T_0}\right)\right],\;}$$ the whole concentric branch of the boxed $f_V$ rescales along the velocity axis by that factor, the force at any fixed shortening speed falls, the isometric force does not, and the peak power falls by the same factor.
By hypothesis $v_{\max}(T)/v_{\max}(T_0) = k_{\text{cyc}}(T)/k_{\text{cyc}}(T_0)$, and by Module 0 Proposition 6.3, $k_{\text{cyc}}(T) = A_{\text{Arr}}\,e^{-E_a/R_gT}$ with the prefactor $A_{\text{Arr}}$ (Module 0’s $A$; not the thick-filament length $A$ of §2) and $E_a$ constant across the interval, so the ratio is $\exp[-(E_a/R_g)(1/T - 1/T_0)]$ — the boxed form. The concentric branch of $f_V$ depends on $v$ only through $v/v_{\max}$, so replacing $v_{\max}$ by a smaller value is a contraction of the curve toward $v = 0$: at any fixed $v \gt 0$ the argument $v/v_{\max}$ grows and $f_V$, which decreases in it, falls; at $v = 0$ the argument is $0$ at either temperature and $f_V = 1$, so $F_0$ is unchanged, as the hypothesis on $F_0$ requires and as Module 0 §6 argues on thermodynamic grounds. Power is $P = F_0\,v\,f_V(v/v_{\max})$; substituting $v = \hat v\,v_{\max}$ gives $P = F_0\,v_{\max}\,\hat v\,f_V(\hat v)$, whose maximum over $\hat v$ is $F_0 v_{\max}$ times a number that depends only on $c$. Hence $P_{\max} \propto v_{\max}$ and scales by the same factor. Where the hypotheses bind: a cycle has several steps with different barriers and the effective $E_a$ is that of whichever step limits at each temperature, so the law holds over an interval in which one step dominates; and $F_0$ is only approximately temperature-independent (it falls by roughly $20$–$30\%$ between $35$ and $20\ ^\circ\mathrm C$ in mammalian fibres — a kinetic loss of attached heads, not a change in the thermodynamic ceiling Module 0 §6 holds fixed), which the proposition sets aside. ∎

Put in the number Module 0 §6 derived. The measured $Q_{10} \approx 2.5$ of crossbridge cycling gives $E_a = 70.0\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, and from body temperature to a cold limb at $25\ ^\circ\mathrm C$ the Arrhenius factor is $0.335$ — every rate a third as fast. So $v_{\max}$ falls from $8$ to $2.68\,\ell_0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and the consequence for force is not small: at a moderate shortening speed of $0.8\,\ell_0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ (a tenth of the warm $v_{\max}$) the warm muscle delivers $0.64\,F_0$ and the cold one $0.32\,F_0$. Half the force, at the same length, activation and speed, with not one crossbridge weaker — and the peak power, $0.095\,F_0v_{\max}$ at $37\ ^\circ\mathrm C$, drops to $0.032$. This is what “a cold muscle is weak” means (the plot below): it is not a weaker spring, it is a slower engine, and the loss is largest exactly where a limb is asked to move.

measured, not derived: the $Q_{10}\approx2.5$ of crossbridge cycling is a fitted steepness, as Module 0 §6’s own marker records; what that module derives from it, by its Proposition 6.3, is $E_a = 70.0\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ and the cooling factor $0.335$, and those two derived numbers are all this section uses, so the threefold factor should be read as “about threefold”.

Proposition 6.2 at two temperatures. Left: the concentric branch of $f_V$ at $37\ ^\circ\mathrm C$ (red) and at $25\ ^\circ\mathrm C$ (blue), where $v_{\max}$ has fallen by the factor $0.335$; the isometric point is shared, and at $0.8\,\ell_0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ the cold force is half the warm one. Right: the power curves, whose peaks stand in the same ratio.

measured, not derived: $v_{\max} = 8\,\ell_0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ (and the $5$–$10$ range of the Appendix) is measured by the slack test on fibres, and this module does not compute it. The rate that would produce it, the detachment step of the cycle at about $10^{3}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$, is itself measured in solution, and the agreement is a consistency check within a factor of two, not a prediction. What Module 0 does supply is its temperature dependence (Proposition 6.2), derived from a measured $Q_{10}$. Module 0’s Proposition 6.4 uses the symbol $v_{\max}$ for a Michaelis–Menten rate; that is not this $v_{\max}$, though the two are related by the argument above.

Power peaks in the middle

Mechanical power is force times velocity, $P=F\,v$. Because force is largest where velocity is smallest and vice versa, their product is small at both ends and largest in between (Fig. 24):

Differentiating Hill’s hyperbola puts the maximum at about $v\approx\tfrac{1}{3}v_{\max}$, where force is about $\tfrac{1}{3}F_0$ and power reaches roughly $0.1\,F_0 v_{\max}$. A muscle asked to deliver power — a cyclist’s legs, a sprinter’s calf — works best not at maximum force nor maximum speed but at this intermediate gear, which is what gear ratios, crank lengths, and cadence choices exist to arrange.

The three factors that scale muscle force are now all in hand: activation $a$ (§3–§5), the length factor $f_L$ (§2), and the velocity factor $f_V$ (here), each riding on the architectural ceiling $F_{\max}$ (§1). §7 assembles them into a single Hill-type muscle model — the synthesis this whole module has been building toward.

7. The Hill-type muscle model

Everything the module has built now meets in one equation. From §1 came the force ceiling $F_{\max}$ and the pennation angle $\theta_p$; from §2 the length factor $f_L(\ell)$; from §3–§5 the activation $a(t)$; from §6 the velocity factor $f_V(v)$. Assembling them into the force a muscle delivers to its tendon is the Hill-type muscle model — the synthesis this module has been driving toward (Fig. 25):

The model has three parts, taken in turn: an active contractile element, a passive elastic element, and the pennation projection onto the tendon.

The contractile element

The contractile element (CE) is the active machinery of §2 — the crossbridges, switched on by calcium. Its force is the ceiling scaled by the three dimensionless factors, exactly the product foreshadowed in §2:

$$F_{CE}(t)=a(t)\,F_{\max}\,f_L(\ell)\,f_V(v).$$

Each factor answers one question about the instant: $a\in[0,1]$, how switched on (§5); $f_L(\ell)\in[0,1]$, how favourable the length (§2); $f_V(v)$, how the shortening speed helps or hurts (§6, and the only factor that can exceed $1$, on the eccentric branch). Multiplied by the architectural ceiling $F_{\max}$ (§1), they give the active tension.

The parallel elastic element

Muscle is not only its crossbridges. The connective tissue wrapping every fibre, fascicle, and the whole belly behaves like a passive spring: stretch the muscle beyond its slack length and it resists, whether or not it is activated. This is the parallel elastic element (PE), carrying a passive tension $F_{PE}(\ell)$ that depends on length alone (Fig. 26):

The curve drawn above is the exponential law the module uses throughout, stated once here so every later figure and lab can be reproduced:

$$\boxed{\;\frac{F_{PE}(\ell)}{F_{\max}}=\begin{cases}0, & \ell\le\ell_0,\\[6pt]\dfrac{e^{\,k_{PE}(\ell/\ell_0-1)/\varepsilon_0}-1}{e^{\,k_{PE}}-1}, & \ell\gt\ell_0,\end{cases}\;}$$

with a shape constant $k_{PE}=3$ and a reference strain $\varepsilon_0=0.6$, both assumed (Appendix). The two constants have a plain reading: $\varepsilon_0$ is the stretch beyond $\ell_0$ at which the passive tension alone equals $F_{\max}$ (here $60\%$, so $\ell=1.6\,\ell_0$, the right-hand edge of the figure), and $k_{PE}$ says how much of that rise is saved for the last part of the stretch. At $\ell=1.2\,\ell_0$ the law gives $F_{PE}=0.090\,F_{\max}$, at $1.4\,\ell_0$ it gives $0.335\,F_{\max}$: passive force is negligible near the optimum and then climbs steeply, like a rubber band taken up past its slack. The element is called parallel because it bears load side by side with the contractile element, so the two tensions simply add. Crucially, it keeps a stretched muscle from going slack on the descending limb: where the active overlap of §2 runs out, passive tension takes over, and the total force a whole muscle exerts stays substantial.

Pennation, the tendon, and one honest assumption

Two steps carry the fibre force to the bone. First, only the tendon-directed component survives the pennation angle, the $\cos\theta_p$ factor of §1. Second, that tension is transmitted through the tendon — and here we make one simplification explicit, because it shapes everything downstream:

Modelling assumption 7.1 (rigid tendon). We treat the tendon as inextensible, so the whole muscle–tendon unit’s length change is taken up entirely by the fibres. Then the fibre length $\ell$ and velocity $v$ follow directly from the joint angle and angular velocity — the model needs no internal force balance, and the labs of §9 can integrate one clean ODE. The tendon’s real compliance — the series-elastic element, which stores and returns energy and lets fibres and tendon move at different speeds — is the first refinement beyond this model, deferred to Module 6.

The assembled model

Adding the passive tension to the active, and projecting onto the tendon, gives the module’s headline result — the whole chain from neural command to tendon force in a single line:

$$\boxed{\;F_{\text{tendon}}=\Big[\,\underbrace{a(t)\,F_{\max}\,f_L(\ell)\,f_V(v)}_{\text{contractile } F_{CE}}\;+\;\underbrace{F_{PE}(\ell)}_{\text{passive}}\,\Big]\cos\theta_p\;}$$

Every symbol has been defined and every factor derived; nothing here is fitted after the fact. The one surface at the model’s core is the product $f_L(\ell)\,f_V(v)$ — force as a joint function of length and velocity, scaled bodily by activation (Fig. 27):

Hand the model an activation $a(t)$ from a neural command, a length $\ell$ and velocity $v$ from the joint’s motion, and it returns the tendon force at that instant. What it does not yet give is the quantity a movement actually cares about — the torque that force produces about the joint, which depends on a moment arm that itself changes with angle, and on antagonist muscles pulling the other way. Converting force to joint torque is §8.

8. From muscle force to joint torque

§7 delivers the tendon force $F_{\text{tendon}}$. But a limb does not care about force in a tendon — it cares about the torque that force produces about a joint, the quantity that actually turns the forearm or extends the knee. Converting one to the other is the last mechanical step, and it repays a debt left open in Module 1.

Force times moment arm

A force produces torque about the joint only through its moment arm — the perpendicular distance from the joint’s axis of rotation to the force’s line of action (Fig. 28):

$$\tau \;=\; F_m\,d_m(\theta),$$

where $F_m$ is the muscle’s tendon force and $d_m$ its moment arm. A worked case pins the scale. Hold a $2\ \mathrm{kg}$ dumbbell with the forearm horizontal and the elbow at $90^\circ$: the weight $W=mg\approx19.6\ \mathrm N$ acts at a load moment arm $r_L\approx0.30\ \mathrm m$ (a shorter grip than §0’s $0.35\ \mathrm m$), needing a joint torque $\tau=W r_L\approx5.9\ \mathrm{N\,m}$. With a biceps moment arm $d_m\approx4\ \mathrm{cm}$, the muscle must pull with $F_m=\tau/d_m\approx147\ \mathrm N$ — the same order as the biceps force estimated in §0, and the direct source of the lever’s force penalty: the muscle’s moment arm is about a seventh of the load’s ($4$ against $30\ \mathrm{cm}$), so it pays about sevenfold in force ($147$ against $19.6\ \mathrm N$).

One number needs reconciling before we go on. §0 took the elbow flexor moment arm as $d_m\approx3\ \mathrm{cm}$, the constant Module 1 carries for its reference human; here it is $4\ \mathrm{cm}$. Both are right, at different angles: Module 1's $3\ \mathrm{cm}$ is a single value chosen to stand for the whole flexion range, while $4\ \mathrm{cm}$ is the peak of the angle-dependent curve of the next subsection, reached near $90^\circ$. Wherever this module quotes a single moment arm it means the value at the stated angle, and the curve $d_m(\theta)$ below supersedes the constant.

The moment arm is not a constant

Module 1 treated $d_m$ as a fixed number — a convenient lie. As a joint rotates, the tendon’s path relative to the axis changes, and with it the moment arm (Fig. 29):

The elbow-flexor moment arm swings from under $2\ \mathrm{cm}$ near full extension to about $4\ \mathrm{cm}$ near $90^\circ$ and back. So the same muscle force yields more than twice the torque at $90^\circ$ as near full extension (about $1.4$ times that at $150^\circ$) — one reason you are strongest with the elbow around a right angle. The joint’s strength is the product of two angle-dependent curves: the muscle’s own force–length–velocity behaviour (§2, §6) and this moment-arm curve. Writing $d_m(\theta)$ rather than a constant is what makes $\tau=F_m\,d_m(\theta)$ honest.

Agonists, antagonists, and co-contraction

Muscles come in opposing groups. An agonist drives a motion (the biceps flexes the elbow); an antagonist opposes it (the triceps extends it). Because they pull in opposite rotational senses, the joint’s net torque is their difference,

$$\tau_{\text{net}} \;=\; \tau_{\text{ago}} - \tau_{\text{anti}} \;=\; F_{\text{ago}}\,d_{\text{ago}} - F_{\text{anti}}\,d_{\text{anti}}.$$

This lets the nervous system do more than set a net torque. Firing agonist and antagonist together — co-contraction — adds their forces at the joint while their torques partly cancel, so the limb barely moves but the joint grows stiff and steady. It is how you hold a full cup on a shaking train, and it costs metabolic energy for no net torque — a trade of efficiency for stability the model makes explicit.

More muscles than the job needs: redundancy

A single joint torque can be produced by many muscles, and usually is: the elbow is flexed by the biceps, the brachialis, and the brachioradialis together. With more muscles than degrees of freedom, the required torque does not determine the individual forces — the problem is redundant, and some further principle must choose. The common modelling choice is that the body spreads the effort to keep every muscle far from its limit, minimising a summed relative stress:

$$\min_{F_i\ge0}\ \sum_i\left(\frac{F_i}{F_{i,\max}}\right)^2 \qquad\text{subject to}\qquad \sum_i F_i\,d_i=\tau.$$

Solved for two elbow flexors sharing the curl torque, this gives a definite split (Fig. 30):

The optimum sends more force to the stronger brachialis than to the biceps — effort is “cheaper” where the capacity is larger. Note the price of sharing: the pair carries $76+114=190\ \mathrm N$ where a single muscle on the $4\ \mathrm{cm}$ arm would need $147\ \mathrm N$, because the brachialis pulls at a shorter arm. Minimising stress is not minimising force. This is only the lightest touch on the redundancy problem: the honest whole-limb version, where the CNS balances dozens of muscles and the very choice of cost function is debated, is deferred to Module 7 (reflex and closed-loop control) and Module 12 (multi-muscle whole-limb models). Even so, the pieces are now complete: a neural command becomes activation (§5), activation and kinematics become muscle force (§7), and force becomes joint torque (here). The next section sets that whole chain running as computer code — §9.

9. Computational labs

The model is now complete enough to run. This section puts it to work in two self-contained Python labs: the first drives a neural command all the way to joint torque; the second adds the fatigue that Module 1 assumed away. Each follows the standard lab structure — question, assumptions, equations, parameters, code, output, interpretation, sensitivity, failure modes, and an extension to try.

Lab 1 — From activation to joint torque

Physical question. Given a time-varying neural command, what elbow torque does the muscle produce through a curl? Biological question. How much does the muscle’s force lag the command, and how do the length and velocity of the moving fibres shape the torque?

Assumptions. A single lumped flexor; rigid tendon (Modelling assumption 7.1), so fibre length and velocity follow the joint angle; a prescribed curl trajectory $\theta(t)$; passive force negligible over this range; activation dynamics as in §5. Equations. The activation ODE $\dot a=(u-a)/\tau_a(u,a)$ (§5), the Hill force $F=a\,F_{\max}f_L(\ell)\,f_V(v)\cos\theta_p$ (§7), and the torque $\tau=F\,d_m(\theta)$ (§8).

Parameters.

SymbolValueMeaning (source)
$F_{\max}$$500\ \mathrm N$peak isometric force of the lumped elbow flexor group; assumed, sitting inside the several hundred newtons §1 estimates for biceps + brachialis + brachioradialis
$\tau_{\text{act}},\ \tau_{\text{deact}}$$10,\ 40\ \mathrm{ms}$activation / deactivation constants (§5)
$v_{\max}$$8\ \ell_0/\mathrm s$maximum shortening velocity (§6)
$\theta_p$$15^\circ$pennation angle (§1)
$\theta(t)$$30^\circ\!\to\!110^\circ$prescribed curl trajectory
$\ell(\theta)/\ell_0$$1-0.003\,(\theta^\circ-70)$fibre length from joint angle; assumed linear, optimal at $\theta=70^\circ$
$d_m(\theta)$$1.8+2.2\sin\theta\ \mathrm{cm}$moment arm; assumed form, peak $4\ \mathrm{cm}$ at $90^\circ$ (§8)

Code.

import numpy as np

# activation ODE constants (s), sec. 5
tau_act, tau_deact = 0.010, 0.040
Fmax, theta_p, vmax = 500.0, np.radians(15), 8.0


def fL(L):  # length factor, sec. 2
    if L <= 0.47 or L >= 1.556:
        return 0.0
    if L < 0.963:
        return (L - 0.47)/0.493
    if L <= 1.0:
        return 1.0
    return (1.556 - L)/0.556


def fV(v):  # velocity factor, sec. 6
    return (1 - v)/(1 + v/0.25) if v >= 0 else 1 + 0.5*20*(-v)/(1 + 20*(-v))


def dm(th):  # moment arm (cm), sec. 8
    return 1.8 + 2.2*np.sin(np.radians(th))


t = np.arange(0, 1.5, 0.001)
u = np.clip((t - 0.1)/0.2, 0, 0.85)
u[t > 0.35] = 0.85

# integrate activation, sec. 5
a = np.zeros_like(t)
for i in range(1, len(t)):
    dt = t[i] - t[i-1]
    tau = tau_act if u[i-1] > a[i-1] else tau_deact
    a[i] = a[i-1] + dt*(u[i-1] - a[i-1])/tau

theta = 30 + 80*np.clip((t - 0.3)/0.7, 0, 1)  # the curl (deg)
L = 1.0 - 0.003*(theta - 70)  # fibre length / l0
# shortening velocity (norm.)
vshort = -np.gradient(L, t)/vmax

fVa = np.array([fV(x) for x in vshort])
F = a*Fmax*np.array([fL(x) for x in L])*fVa*np.cos(theta_p)
tau = F*np.array([dm(x) for x in theta])/100.0  # joint torque (N m)
print(f"peak torque {tau.max():.1f} N m at t = {t[tau.argmax()]:.2f} s")

Output. Running it prints peak torque 13.4 N m at t = 0.76 s and produces the two time series (Fig. 31):

Interpretation. The activation visibly lags the command on the rise (the $\tau_{\text{act}}$ delay), and the torque lags further still, because force must build after activation and then be geared through the moment arm. The small dip as the curl begins is the velocity factor $f_V$ biting: once the fibres start shortening, force drops before the growing moment arm near $90^\circ$ wins it back. Sensitivity. Torque scales linearly with $F_{\max}$; a larger $\tau_{\text{act}}$ delays and blunts the rise; a faster curl (smaller movement time) cuts peak force through $f_V$. Failure modes. With a rigid tendon the model cannot show tendon energy storage or the electromechanical delay’s elastic component; a very fast movement would push $v$ toward $v_{\max}$ where the Euler step needs shrinking. Extension. Swap the elbow parameters for the quadriceps–knee or the calf–Achilles–ankle (larger $F_{\max}$, different $d_m(\theta)$) and compare the torque a comparable command produces at each joint.

Lab 2 — Fatigue-sensitive force

Physical question. Why does the same neural command produce less force the longer it is held? Biological question. How fast does force fade under sustained effort, and how slowly does it come back?

Assumptions. Isometric hold (fixed length and velocity, so $f_L=f_V=1$); a single fatigue state variable $C\in[0,1]$ — the fraction of contractile capacity still available — that is depleted in proportion to activation and recovers toward $1$ when rested; activation quasi-static on the fatigue timescale (seconds, versus milliseconds for $a$). Equations. $\dot C=-F_f\,a\,C+F_r\,(1-C)$, with realised force $F\propto a\,C$. This is the minimal repayment of Module 1’s “unlimited force” idealisation; the physiological three-compartment version is Module 14.

Parameters. Fatigue rate $F_f=0.018\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$, recovery rate $F_r=0.020\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$; command $u=0.9$ held for $60\ \mathrm s$, then released.

Code.

import numpy as np

Ff, Fr = 0.018, 0.020  # fatigue and recovery rates (1/s)
t = np.arange(0, 120, 0.05)
u = np.where(t < 60, 0.9, 0.0)  # 60 s effort, then release
a = u.copy()  # activation quasi-static at this timescale

C = np.ones_like(t)  # available contractile capacity
for i in range(1, len(t)):
    dt = t[i] - t[i-1]
    C[i] = C[i-1] + dt*(-Ff*a[i-1]*C[i-1] + Fr*(1 - C[i-1]))

force = a*C  # normalised isometric force
print(f"force at 60 s: {force[t < 60][-1]:.2f}; capacity min {C.min():.2f}")

Output. It prints force at 60 s: 0.54; capacity min 0.60 and the fatigue–recovery curves (Fig. 32):

Interpretation. Activation holds flat, yet force falls by $40\%$ within a minute, purely because capacity $C$ drains — the model reproduces fatigue without any change in the command. Releasing the effort lets $C$ climb back over tens of seconds; recovery here takes about as long as the fade because we chose $F_r\approx F_f$, whereas real muscle recovers faster than it fatigues after submaximal work. Sensitivity. Setting $\dot C=0$ gives the steady capacity $C_\infty=F_r/(F_r+F_f\,a)$, so the steady force is $a\,C_\infty$: at $a=0.9$ that is $C_\infty=0.55$ and a force of $0.50$, below the $0.54$ the run reaches at $60\ \mathrm s$ because the hold ends before the capacity has settled. Raise $F_f$ and it fatigues deeper; raise $F_r$ and it holds up better. Failure modes. One lumped $C$ cannot capture the different fatigue rates of slow versus fast motor units (§4), nor metabolic recovery kinetics; those need the multi-compartment model of Module 14. Extension. Give the fast (fatigable) and slow (resistant) motor-unit pools of §4 separate $C$ variables and recruit them by the size principle, so a long low effort fatigues far less than a short maximal one.

With the model exercised end to end, the last section takes honest stock of what it captures and what it leaves out, and closes with problems — §10.

10. What the model captures and misses; diagnostics and problems

The Hill-type model earns its place by turning a neural command into joint torque with a handful of measured constants and no free curve-fitting. It is worth being just as clear about what it leaves out — each idealisation is honest, and each is repaid in a later module (Fig. 33).

What it captures. The length–tension law (§2), the calcium-set activation with its asymmetric rise and fall (§3–§5), the force–velocity hyperbola with its strong eccentric branch (§6), pennation and the architectural force ceiling (§1), the angle-dependent moment arm and agonist–antagonist torque (§8), and — lightly — redundancy and fatigue (§8, §9). That is enough to predict, moment by moment, the torque a muscle produces and why it fades.

What it idealises, and where it is repaid:

Idealisation (in this module)What it omitsRepaid in
Rigid tendon (Assumption 7.1)elastic energy storage & return; fibre–tendon speed differenceModule 6 (series-elastic element)
Neural drive $u$ prescribed by hand (§5)reflexes, muscle spindles, closed-loop control, co-contraction strategyModule 7
Redundancy shown for two muscles (§8)whole-limb load-sharing across dozens of muscles; the cost-function debateModule 7, Module 12
One lumped fatigue state (§9)fibre-type-specific fatigue, metabolic and recovery kinetics, ageingModule 14
Prescribed joint kinematics (§9)limb inertia and forward dynamics (torque $\to$ motion); the module stays on Level 5 of the level ladder and computes no Level‑2 planar rigid-body result except in K7later dynamics module

How the model is measured and validated

Every quantity in the model maps to a laboratory measurement, which is what keeps it falsifiable:

  • Activation $a$ — surface or intramuscular EMG, the electrical shadow of the motor-unit firing of §4, processed into an activation estimate.
  • Joint torque $\tau$ — an isokinetic dynamometer, which holds a joint’s angular velocity and reads the torque directly, tracing the force–velocity and torque–angle curves in the intact limb.
  • Fascicle length $\ell$ and pennation $\theta_p$ — B-mode ultrasound, which images the fibres shortening and rotating in real time during a contraction.
  • $F_{\max}$ and PCSA — muscle volume from MRI combined with ultrasound architecture (§1).

Diagnostics

Five quick self-checks. Answer each before opening the solution; if any is unclear, the linked section is where to look.

  1. Why does muscle force lag the neural command, and outlast it?
    Solution
    Activation follows the command through a first-order ODE with a time constant (§5), and calcium is released fast (channel) but cleared slowly (pump), so $\tau_{\text{act}}\approx10\ \mathrm{ms}\lt\tau_{\text{deact}}\approx40\ \mathrm{ms}$: force builds after the command and lingers after it stops.
  2. A single twitch reaches only about a fifth of full activation. How does the body get a strong, smooth contraction?
    Solution
    Two knobs (§4): recruit more motor units (small before large, by the size principle) and fire each faster so the twitches sum into a fused tetanus.
  3. Why can you lower a weight you could never lift?
    Solution
    Lowering is eccentric (the muscle lengthens under load), and on the eccentric branch of the force–velocity curve force rises above $F_0$, to roughly $1.5\,F_0$ (§6).
  4. Why are you strongest with the elbow near a right angle?
    Solution
    Two angle-dependent factors peak near mid-range: the sarcomere length factor $f_L$ sits near its plateau (§2), and the moment arm $d_m(\theta)$ is largest around $90^\circ$ (§8). Their product is the joint’s strength curve.
  5. You hold a steady contraction and the force fades, though you feel you are trying just as hard. Why?
    Solution
    The command (and activation) can stay constant while the available contractile capacity $C$ drains under sustained effort (§9, Lab 2); realised force is $a\cdot C$, so it sags even with $a$ unchanged.

Problems

Thirty-one problems in three strands — conceptual (C1–C10), derivational (D1–D10), and computational (K1–K11) — each with a worked solution; the computational answers are Python-verified. A Probes note names what each tests. The map below shows which section each problem draws on — and, read by row, that every section is exercised:

SectionConceptualDerivationalComputational
§1 architecture & pennationC3D1K1
§2 sarcomere / length–tensionC1, C2D2K6
§3–§5 activationC4, C6D6K5, K10, K11
§4 motor units & tetanusC5D10K2
§6 force–velocity & powerC7D3, D4, D5K3, K4
§7 Hill model——K7
§8 torque & redundancyC8, C9D8, D9K8
§9 labs & fatigueC10D7K9

Conceptual (C1–C10)

C1. Why is the sarcomere, not the whole muscle, the natural unit for the length–tension law? Probes: the hierarchy of §1 and the overlap geometry of §2.
Solution
Force depends on length only because thick/thin filament overlap does, and overlap is a property of the single sarcomere. A whole muscle is millions of sarcomeres in series and parallel; its curve is the sarcomere curve with the kinks averaged out.
C2. A fully activated muscle produces zero active force at certain lengths. Name one and say why. Probes: §2.
Solution
At $\ell\ge4.20\ \mu\mathrm m$ the thin and thick filaments no longer overlap, so no crossbridge can attach and active force is zero regardless of activation (likewise below $\approx1.27\ \mu\mathrm m$, where the filaments jam).
C3. A pennate muscle pays a $\cos\theta_p$ force penalty, yet the body’s strongest muscles are pennate. Explain. Probes: §1.
Solution
Angling the fibres lets many more (shorter) fibres pack into the same volume, raising the physiological cross-section (PCSA). Since $F_{\max}=\sigma\,\mathrm{PCSA}\cos\theta_p$ and the PCSA gain outruns the modest $\cos\theta_p$ loss, pennation is a high-force design — at the cost of range.
C4. One twitch reaches only $a\approx0.22$. How does the nervous system reach a strong, smooth contraction? Probes: §3–§4.
Solution
By firing fast enough that successive twitches sum before activation can relax — a fused tetanus at the ceiling $a_\infty\approx0.73$ — and by recruiting more motor units. Rate coding and recruitment together.
C5. In what order are motor units recruited, and why can the CNS not simply choose to fire a large one first? Probes: §4.
Solution
Smallest first (the size principle). A small motoneuron has high input resistance, so a shared synaptic current depolarises it most ($\Delta V=IR$) and it reaches threshold first. The order is forced by cell size, not selectable.
C6. Why does force lag the command when a contraction starts and linger after it ends? Probes: §5.
Solution
Activation obeys a first-order ODE with asymmetric constants: calcium floods in fast through a channel ($\tau_{\text{act}}\approx10\ \mathrm{ms}$) but is pumped out slowly ($\tau_{\text{deact}}\approx40\ \mathrm{ms}$), so $a$ rises quickly yet falls slowly.
C7. You can lower a weight you could never lift. Which part of the model explains it? Probes: §6.
Solution
Lowering is eccentric (the muscle lengthens under load). On the eccentric branch of the force–velocity curve force rises above the isometric $F_0$, to roughly $1.5\,F_0$.
C8. Two flexors can supply a required elbow torque in infinitely many ways. What principle picks one, and whom does it favour? Probes: §8.
Solution
Minimising summed relative stress $\sum(F_i/F_{i,\max})^2$ subject to the torque constraint. It sends more force to the muscle with the larger capacity (and/or larger moment arm) — effort is cheaper where there is more of it.
C9. Co-contracting agonist and antagonist costs metabolic energy but yields no net joint torque. What is the point? Probes: §8.
Solution
It raises joint stiffness and stability: the opposing torques cancel while both muscles resist perturbations, steadying the limb (e.g. holding a full cup on a moving train).
C10. During a sustained hold the force fades although you feel you are trying equally hard. Which model variable is changing, and which is not? Probes: §9.
Solution
Activation $a$ (the command) stays roughly constant; the fatigue capacity $C$ falls. Realised force is $a\cdot C$, so it droops even though the command is unchanged.

Derivational (D1–D10)

D1. Derive the architectural force ceiling $F_{\max}=\sigma\,\mathrm{PCSA}\,\cos\theta_p$. Probes: §1.
Solution
Each unit of fibre cross-section pulls with stress $\sigma$, so the fibres’ own force is $F_{\text{fibre}}=\sigma\,\mathrm{PCSA}$ along their direction. Resolving onto the tendon keeps only the component $\cos\theta_p$, giving $F_{\max}=\sigma\,\mathrm{PCSA}\cos\theta_p$.
D2. Derive the straight descending limb of $f_L(\ell)$ from overlap geometry, and its zero. Probes: §2.
Solution
On the descending limb overlap is $\tfrac{A}{2}-(\tfrac{\ell}{2}-a_{\text{thin}})$, linear in $\ell$; normalising by the head-bearing half-length gives $f_L=\dfrac{4.20-\ell}{4.20-2.70}$, which reaches zero when the thin filaments clear the thick, at $\ell=A+2a_{\text{thin}}=4.20\ \mu\mathrm m$.
D3. From Hill’s equation $(F+a_H)(v+b_H)=(F_0+a_H)b_H$, show the shortening velocity at zero force is $v_{\max}=b_H F_0/a_H$. Probes: §6.
Solution
Set $F=0$: $a_H(v+b_H)=(F_0+a_H)b_H\Rightarrow a_H v = F_0 b_H\Rightarrow v=v_{\max}=b_H F_0/a_H$.
D4. Reduce Hill’s equation to the normalised concentric factor $f_V=\dfrac{1-v/v_{\max}}{1+v/(c\,v_{\max})}$ with $c=a_H/F_0$. Probes: §6.
Solution
Solve for $F$: $F=\dfrac{(F_0+a_H)b_H}{v+b_H}-a_H=\dfrac{F_0 b_H-a_H v}{v+b_H}$. Divide by $F_0$, use $b_H=c\,v_{\max}$ and $a_H=cF_0$: $f_V=\dfrac{c\,v_{\max}-c\,v}{v+c\,v_{\max}}=\dfrac{1-v/v_{\max}}{1+v/(c\,v_{\max})}$.
D5. Show that concentric power $P=F\,v$ for Hill’s curve peaks at an intermediate velocity (set $dP/dv=0$). Probes: §6.
Solution
With $F\propto\dfrac{v_{\max}-v}{v+c\,v_{\max}}$, $P\propto\dfrac{v(v_{\max}-v)}{v+c\,v_{\max}}$. Setting $dP/dv=0$ gives a quadratic whose positive root lies strictly between $0$ and $v_{\max}$; for $c=0.25$ it is $v\approx0.31\,v_{\max}$, where $F\approx0.31F_0$ — the familiar “one-third” rule.
D6. Solve the activation ODE $\dot a=(u-a)/\tau$ for a constant command $u$ from $a(0)=a_0$. Probes: §5.
Solution
Linear first-order: $a(t)=u+(a_0-u)e^{-t/\tau}$. It relaxes exponentially to $u$ with time constant $\tau$ — $\tau_{\text{act}}$ if $u\gt a$, else $\tau_{\text{deact}}$.
D7. Derive the steady force under a sustained command from the fatigue model $\dot C=-F_f a C+F_r(1-C)$. Probes: §9.
Solution
Set $\dot C=0$: $F_r(1-C)=F_f aC\Rightarrow C_\infty=\dfrac{F_r}{F_r+F_f a}$. Realised steady force is $a\,C_\infty=\dfrac{a\,F_r}{F_r+F_f a}$, below the unfatigued $a$.
D8. A muscle spans a joint with origin and insertion at distances $r_1$ and $r_2$ from the axis, enclosing angle $\gamma$. Derive its moment arm. Probes: §8.
Solution
The muscle length is $L=\sqrt{r_1^2+r_2^2-2r_1r_2\cos\gamma}$ (law of cosines). The moment arm is the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action; using the triangle area two ways, $\tfrac12 r_1r_2\sin\gamma=\tfrac12 L\,d_m$, so $d_m=\dfrac{r_1r_2\sin\gamma}{L}$ — which peaks at intermediate $\gamma$, as the elbow curve of §8 shows.
D9. Using a Lagrange multiplier, show the redundancy optimum has $F_i\propto d_i F_{i,\max}^2$. Probes: §8.
Solution
Minimise $\sum(F_i/F_{i,\max})^2-\lambda(\sum F_i d_i-\tau)$. Setting the derivative in $F_i$ to zero: $2F_i/F_{i,\max}^2=\lambda d_i$, so $F_i=\tfrac{\lambda}{2}d_i F_{i,\max}^2$. The shared $\lambda$ is fixed by the torque constraint; force scales with moment arm times capacity-squared.
D10. Show that as firing rate $\to\infty$ the tetanic activation approaches the calcium ceiling $a_\infty$. Probes: §4–§5.
Solution
At high rate the saturating calcium gate stays pinned at its peak, so the target $a_\infty$ is held constant. The ODE $\dot a=(a_\infty-a)/\tau_a$ then drives $a\to a_\infty$; the ripple $\propto$ the inter-pulse decay vanishes as the interval $\to0$. Hence fused tetanus $=a_\infty\approx0.73$.

Computational (K1–K10)

These require genuine computation — simulation, optimisation, an inverse problem, or a sensitivity sweep — not substitution into a boxed formula. Every number below was printed by the code shown with the problem: each of K1–K10 now carries a runnable block, and each block prints the quantities its solution quotes.

K1. A muscle of fixed volume $V$ and belly thickness $h$ can trade pennation for packing: a fibre of length $\ell_f=h/\sin\theta_p$ gives a physiological cross-section $\mathrm{PCSA}=V/\ell_f$. Numerically maximise the tendon force $F_{\max}(\theta_p)=\sigma\,\mathrm{PCSA}\cos\theta_p$ over $\theta_p$; report the force gained over a typical $20^\circ$ muscle and the excursion lost, and explain why real muscles stop short of the optimum. Probes: §1; constrained optimisation (argmax).
Solution
Substituting, $F_{\max}\propto\sin\theta_p\cos\theta_p=\tfrac12\sin2\theta_p$, maximal at $\boxed{\theta_p=45^\circ}$. Going $20^\circ\!\to\!45^\circ$ multiplies force by $\sin90^\circ/\sin40^\circ=\mathbf{1.56}$ (+56%). But the fibre length $\ell_f=h/\sin\theta_p$ shrinks by $\sin20^\circ/\sin45^\circ=\mathbf{0.48}$ — halving the shortening range. Real muscles ($\theta_p\approx20$–$30^\circ$) sit well below the force optimum because they also need excursion: architecture optimises force and range together, not force alone. 
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize_scalar

SIG = 0.3e6           # Pa, specific tension, sec. 1
VOL, THK = 2.0e-4, 0.02   # m^3 and m: belly volume and thickness


def force(th):
    """Tendon force for pennation th (rad), fixed volume and thickness."""
    ell_f = THK / np.sin(th)
    return SIG * (VOL / ell_f) * np.cos(th)


r = minimize_scalar(lambda t: -force(t), bounds=(0.05, 1.5),
                    method="bounded")
opt = np.degrees(r.x)
print(f"optimum pennation = {opt:.1f} deg")
print(f"force gain 20 deg -> optimum = "
      f"{force(r.x) / force(np.radians(20)):.2f}x")
print(f"fibre length ratio = "
      f"{np.sin(np.radians(20)) / np.sin(r.x):.2f}")
K2. Simulate the twitch-summation model of §4 (saturating calcium gate + activation ODE) for impulse trains from $5$ to $80\ \mathrm{Hz}$; for each rate compute the steady peak-to-trough ripple relative to the mean, and locate the fusion frequency where it drops below $5\%$. Repeat for a slow fibre whose twitch is $\sim\!2.5\times$ longer. Report both. Probes: §4; numerical simulation of the model.
Solution
The code below integrates Modelling assumption 3.2 for each rate. It reproduces the three traces of Fig. 15 (mean activation $0.147$, $0.380$ and $0.688$ at $10$, $25$ and $60\ \mathrm{Hz}$) and then sweeps the rate: 
import numpy as np

TR, TD, TAU_A = 3.6, 18.0, 41.0   # ms: Ca release, Ca re-uptake, activation
T_PK = TR * np.log(1 + TD / TR)   # peak time of the raw two-exponential shape
NORM = (1 - np.exp(-T_PK / TR)) * np.exp(-T_PK / TD)


def pulse(t, s=1.0):
    """Normalised single-pulse calcium shape, sec. 3, stretched by s."""
    tt = np.clip(t, 0.0, None)
    y = (1 - np.exp(-tt / (TR * s))) * np.exp(-tt / (TD * s))
    return np.where(t > 0, y / NORM, 0.0)


def train(f, s=1.0, T=1200.0, dt=0.1):
    """Mean activation and relative ripple for an f Hz impulse train."""
    t = np.arange(0.0, T, dt)
    prod = np.ones_like(t)
    for ti in np.arange(0.0, T, 1000.0 / f):
        prod *= 1 - pulse(t - ti, s)
    ca = 0.1 + 1.3 * (1 - prod)          # micromolar, sec. 3
    tgt = ca**3 / (1 + ca**3)            # Hill, n = 3, Ca50 = 1 micromolar
    a = np.zeros_like(t)
    for i in range(1, len(t)):
        a[i] = a[i - 1] + dt * (tgt[i - 1] - a[i - 1]) / (TAU_A * s)
    w = t > 0.6 * T
    return a[w].mean(), (a[w].max() - a[w].min()) / a[w].mean()


for rate in (10.0, 25.0, 60.0):
    m, rip = train(rate)
    print(f"{rate:4.0f} Hz: mean a {m:.3f}, ripple {100 * rip:.0f}%")
for s, name in ((1.0, "fast"), (2.5, "slow")):
    for f in np.arange(5.0, 90.01, 0.5):
        if train(f, s)[1] < 0.05:
            print(f"{name} fibre: fusion frequency {f:.1f} Hz")
            break

The ripple falls below $5\%$ at $\boxed{42.5\ \mathrm{Hz}}$ for the fast fibre and $\boxed{17.0\ \mathrm{Hz}}$ for the slow one — the ${\approx}42\ \mathrm{Hz}$ Fig. 17 marks, and a rate two and a half times lower for a twitch two and a half times longer. Fusion tracks $1/(\text{twitch duration})$, so slower fibres fuse at lower rates, which is why the nervous system can rate-code fast (fatigable) units over a much wider frequency band than slow ones. Note what the sweep does that the boxed relations cannot: the fusion frequency is not any single model constant, it is the rate at which a nonlinear saturating gate and a first-order filter stop leaving a gap.

K3. Numerically maximise the concentric power $P(v)=f_V(v)\,v$; then sweep the Hill curvature $c=a_H/F_0\in\{0.1,0.25,0.5\}$ and report how the optimal velocity $v^\ast/v_{\max}$ and the peak power move. Probes: §6; numerical optimisation + sensitivity sweep.
Solution
The optima are $c=0.1\!:v^\ast=0.23,\,P^\ast=0.054$; $c=0.25\!:v^\ast=0.31,\,P^\ast=0.095$; $c=0.5\!:v^\ast=0.37,\,P^\ast=0.134$ (in units of $F_0v_{\max}$). A straighter hyperbola (larger $c$) pushes the power optimum to higher velocity and multiplies peak power by 2.5 ($0.134/0.054$). This quantifies the fibre-type story: fast fibres, with a less-curved $f_V$, are the powerful ones — a fact the boxed $f_V$ alone does not reveal. 
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize_scalar


def power(v, c):
    """Normalised concentric power f_V(v) * v, in units of F0 * vmax."""
    return (1 - v) / (1 + v / c) * v


for c in (0.10, 0.25, 0.50):
    r = minimize_scalar(lambda v: -power(v, c), bounds=(1e-4, 0.999),
                        method="bounded")
    print(f"c = {c:.2f}: v* = {r.x:.2f} vmax, "
          f"P* = {power(r.x, c):.3f} F0 vmax")
K4. Sweep the speed $|v|/v_{\max}$ from $0$ to $1$ and, at each speed, compute the eccentric-to-concentric force ratio $f_V(-v)/f_V(v)$ — which is also the ratio of the mechanical work done over a fixed excursion $|\Delta\ell|$. Report the ratio at $|v|=0.1$, $0.3$, $0.5$, $0.7$ and $0.9$, find the speed at which it first reaches $3$, and evaluate both limits: as $v\to0$ and as $v\to v_{\max}$. Then say what the two limits mean physically, and why a metabolic conclusion cannot be read off this curve alone. Probes: §6; sensitivity sweep + limit analysis.
Solution
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import brentq

C, K, FECC = 0.25, 20.0, 1.5      # curvature, shape constant, plateau


def fV(v):
    """Normalised force at normalised velocity v (positive = shortening)."""
    if v >= 0:
        return (1 - v) / (1 + v / C)
    return 1 + (FECC - 1) * K * (-v) / (1 + K * (-v))


def ratio(v):
    """Eccentric force divided by concentric force at the same speed."""
    return fV(-v) / fV(v)


for v in (0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9):
    print(f"|v| = {v}: concentric {fV(v):.3f}, eccentric {fV(-v):.3f}, "
          f"ratio {ratio(v):5.2f}, work ratio {ratio(v):5.2f}")
print(f"ratio = 3 at |v| = {brentq(lambda v: ratio(v) - 3, 1e-6, 0.99):.2f}")
small = 1e-4
print(f"limit v -> 0 : {ratio(small):.4f} "
      f"(slope ratio {(fV(-small) - 1) / (1 - fV(small)):.2f})")
print(f"limit v -> 1 : concentric {fV(1 - 1e-6):.2e}, ratio diverges")

At $|v|=0.3$ the familiar pair appears: $f_V=0.318$ concentric against $1.429$ eccentric, so eccentric action bears $\mathbf{4.49\times}$ the force and does $4.49\times$ the (negative) work over the same excursion. But the sweep is the point. The ratio is $2.07$ at $|v|=0.1$, $8.73$ at $0.5$, $18.6$ at $0.7$ and $\mathbf{67.8}$ at $0.9$, first reaching $3$ at $|v|=\mathbf{0.19}$, and the two limits explain the shape. As $v\to0$ the ratio $\to1$: at zero speed there is only one force, $F_0$, and the asymmetry is entirely in the slopes — the printed slope ratio is exactly $2.00$, the relation that fixed $k=20$ in §6. As $v\to v_{\max}$ the concentric branch goes to zero while the eccentric branch is still climbing toward its $1.5$ plateau, so the ratio diverges: at high speed a muscle can resist a load it cannot move at all. That divergence, not the single number at $0.3$, is why lowering a weight you cannot lift is possible for every weight between $F_0$ and $1.5F_0$.

The metabolic conclusion does not follow from this curve. Force ratio is not cost ratio: the sweep says nothing about how much ATP a bridge consumes, and the work per unit tension-time integral is $|v|\,v_{\max}$ in both directions, so the mechanical bookkeeping alone cannot separate them. The extra ingredient is an assumption from Hill's heat measurements ($\S6$): ATP is spent on the cycling powerstroke, and during forced lengthening a bridge is pulled off mechanically rather than released by a powerstroke, so its cycling cost is largely absent. Granting that assumption, eccentric work is cheap (walking downhill, lowering loads), and, because so much force runs through so few attached bridges, it is also the most damaging.

K5. Invert the activation ODE ($u=a+\tau_a\dot a$) to find the command that drives a linear activation ramp to $a=0.9$ in a rise time $T_r$ (use $\tau_{\text{act}}=10\ \mathrm{ms}$). Find the minimum $T_r$ for which the command stays $u\le1$, and interpret. Probes: §5; inverse problem (deconvolution).
Solution
For a linear ramp $\dot a=0.9/T_r$, so $u(t)=a(t)+\tau_{\text{act}}(0.9/T_r)$, peaking at $t=T_r$ with $u=0.9+0.9\tau_{\text{act}}/T_r$. Requiring $u\le1$ gives $\boxed{T_r\ge9\,\tau_{\text{act}}=90\ \mathrm{ms}}$. A $20\ \mathrm{ms}$ ramp would demand $u=\mathbf{1.35}$ — impossible. The muscle’s activation bandwidth ($\sim\!\tau_{\text{act}}$) caps how fast force can be commanded; faster movements must exploit stored tendon elasticity or pre-activation, not a bigger command. 
import numpy as np

TAU_ACT, A_END = 0.010, 0.9        # s and the activation the ramp reaches


def command_peak(t_r):
    """Peak command u for a linear ramp to A_END in rise time t_r."""
    return A_END + TAU_ACT * A_END / t_r


t_min = TAU_ACT * A_END / (1 - A_END)
print(f"minimum rise time = {1e3 * t_min:.0f} ms = "
      f"{t_min / TAU_ACT:.0f} tau_act")
print(f"command needed for a 20 ms ramp = {command_peak(0.020):.2f}")
grid = np.linspace(0.02, 0.20, 10)
print("t_r (ms), u_peak:",
      ", ".join(f"{1e3 * t:.0f}:{command_peak(t):.2f}" for t in grid))
K6. Through a curl $\theta:30^\circ\!\to\!110^\circ$, compute the fibre length $\ell(\theta)$ and the joint-strength product $f_L(\ell)\,d_m(\theta)$ across the range. Find the angle of peak joint strength and compare it to the angles of peak $f_L$ and peak moment arm. Probes: §2, §8; integration over a trajectory.
Solution
import numpy as np


def fL(x):
    """Active length factor at normalised fibre length x (Lab 1)."""
    if x <= 0.47 or x >= 1.556:
        return 0.0
    if x < 0.963:
        return (x - 0.47) / 0.493
    if x <= 1.0:
        return 1.0
    return (1.556 - x) / 0.556


th = np.linspace(30.0, 110.0, 8001)
ell = 1.0 - 0.003 * (th - 70.0)
strength = np.array([fL(x) for x in ell]) * (1.8 + 2.2 * np.sin(
    np.radians(th)))
plateau = th[(ell >= 0.963) & (ell <= 1.0)]
print(f"fL plateau spans theta = {plateau.min():.1f} to "
      f"{plateau.max():.1f} deg")
print(f"moment arm peaks at theta = 90 deg")
print(f"strength peaks at theta = {th[strength.argmax()]:.1f} deg, "
      f"value {strength.max():.3f} cm")

With $\ell(\theta)/\ell_0=1-0.003(\theta^\circ-70)$ the fibre sits at $\ell_0$ at $\theta=70^\circ$ and stays on the length–tension plateau ($0.963\le\ell/\ell_0\le1$) all the way to $\theta=82.3^\circ$; below $70^\circ$ it is on the descending limb and above $82.3^\circ$ on the ascending limb. The moment arm $d_m=1.8+2.2\sin\theta$ rises monotonically to $90^\circ$. So on $[70^\circ,82.3^\circ]$ the product is $1\times d_m(\theta)$, still rising, and beyond $82.3^\circ$ the falling $f_L$ beats the flattening $d_m$: the strength peaks at $\boxed{82.3^\circ}$, at $3.98\ \mathrm{cm}$ of effective arm, the far edge of the plateau. The lesson is not that neither factor is maximal there — $f_L$ is at its maximum across the whole plateau — but that a flat factor hands the choice of optimum entirely to the other one. Read either curve alone and you would place the strongest angle at $70^\circ$ or at $90^\circ$; both are wrong.

K7. Hang a limb on the assembled model of §7 and compare it with the constant-torque shortcut. Take an elbow angle $\theta$ measured from full extension, inertia $I_J=0.06\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$, passive joint stiffness $k_J=9.6\ \mathrm{N\,m\,rad^{-1}}$ and damping $b_J=0.76\ \mathrm{N\,m\,s\,rad^{-1}}$ (all assumed), with $\ell(\theta)$, $d_m(\theta)$, $F_{\max}=500\ \mathrm N$, $\theta_p=15^\circ$ and $v_{\max}=8\,\ell_0\,\mathrm s^{-1}$ from Lab 1 and the passive element of §7, so that $$F_{\text{tendon}}=\big[a\,F_{\max}f_L(\ell)\,f_V(v)+F_{\max}f_{PE}(\ell)\big]\cos\theta_p .$$ Integrate $$\dot a=\frac{u-a}{\tau_a(u,a)},\qquad I_J\ddot\theta=F_{\text{tendon}}\,d_m(\theta)-k_J\theta-b_J\dot\theta$$ from rest for a step command $u=0.6$, then integrate the same limb driven instead by $\tau=a\,\tau_{\max}$ with $\tau_{\max}=14\ \mathrm{N\,m}$. Report the equilibrium angle (confirm it by root-finding on the torque balance), the overshoot and the settling time for each, and say which of the model's factors accounts for the difference. Probes: §7, §8; coupled ODE integration + regime comparison.
Solution
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import brentq

FMAX, CP, VMAX = 500.0, np.cos(np.radians(15.0)), 8.0
KJ, BJ, IJ, TMAX, U = 9.6, 0.76, 0.06, 14.0, 0.6
TAU_ACT, TAU_DEACT = 0.010, 0.040


def fL(x):
    if x <= 0.47 or x >= 1.556:
        return 0.0
    if x < 0.963:
        return (x - 0.47) / 0.493
    if x <= 1.0:
        return 1.0
    return (1.556 - x) / 0.556


def fV(v):
    if v >= 0:
        return (1 - v) / (1 + v / 0.25)
    return 1 + 0.5 * 20 * (-v) / (1 + 20 * (-v))


def fPE(x):
    return (np.exp(3 * max(x - 1.0, 0.0) / 0.6) - 1) / (np.e**3 - 1)


def torque(a, th, om):
    """Assembled Hill torque (N m) at activation a, angle th, rate om."""
    x = 1.0 - 0.003 * (np.degrees(th) - 70.0)
    v = 0.003 * np.degrees(om) / VMAX
    force = (a * FMAX * fL(x) * fV(v) + FMAX * fPE(x)) * CP
    return force * (1.8 + 2.2 * np.sin(th)) / 100.0


def run(kind, dt=2e-5, t_end=3.0):
    n = int(t_end / dt)
    a = th = om = 0.0
    hist = np.empty(n)
    for i in range(n):
        a += dt * (U - a) / (TAU_ACT if U > a else TAU_DEACT)
        tq = a * TMAX if kind == "const" else torque(a, th, om)
        om += dt * (tq - KJ * th - BJ * om) / IJ
        th += dt * om
        hist[i] = np.degrees(th)
    t = np.arange(n) * dt
    eq = hist[-1]
    out = np.where(np.abs(hist - eq) > 0.02 * eq)[0]
    return eq, 100 * max(hist.max() - eq, 0.0) / eq, t[out[-1]]


for kind in ("const", "hill"):
    eq, ov, ts = run(kind)
    print(f"{kind:5s}: equilibrium {eq:.1f} deg, overshoot {ov:.1f}%, "
          f"settling {ts:.2f} s")
root = brentq(lambda x: torque(U, x, 0.0) - KJ * x, 0.05, 1.5)
slope = (torque(U, root + 0.05, 0.0) - torque(U, root - 0.05, 0.0)) / 0.10
print(f"root-find equilibrium {np.degrees(root):.2f} deg")
print(f"torque-angle slope {slope:.2f}, effective stiffness "
      f"{KJ - slope:.2f} N m/rad")
print(f"zeta: constant torque {BJ / (2 * np.sqrt(KJ * IJ)):.2f}, "
      f"reduced stiffness {BJ / (2 * np.sqrt((KJ - slope) * IJ)):.2f}")

The shortcut is a linear second-order system. Its equilibrium is $\theta=0.6(14)/9.6=0.875\ \mathrm{rad}=\mathbf{50.1^\circ}$, and with damping ratio $\zeta=b_J/(2\sqrt{k_JI_J})=0.50$ it overshoots by $\mathbf{16.1\%}$ and settles inside $2\%$ at $\mathbf{0.65\ s}$. The assembled model differs in both respects. Its torque grows with angle, because $f_L$ climbs toward the plateau and $d_m$ toward $90^\circ$: the torque–angle slope at the operating point is $5.24\ \mathrm{N\,m\,rad^{-1}}$, which subtracts from $k_J$ and leaves an effective stiffness of only $4.36\ \mathrm{N\,m\,rad^{-1}}$, so the equilibrium moves out to $\mathbf{63.4^\circ}$ (root-finding on $F_{\text{tendon}}d_m=k_J\theta$ gives $63.45^\circ$). And $f_V$ is a velocity-dependent brake: shortening cuts force, so the muscle supplies damping the shortcut has no way to represent. The two effects together take the response over the critical line — the reduced stiffness alone raises $\zeta$ to $0.74$, and $f_V$ does the rest — so the assembled model reaches equilibrium with no overshoot at all, settling at $\mathbf{1.47\ s}$. The lesson is that a muscle is not a torque source with a spring bolted on: the force–length and force–velocity laws of §2 and §6 make it a low-level controller in its own right, and the overshoot the constant-torque model predicts is an artefact of discarding them. This is also the step the prescribed-kinematics labs of §9 skipped, and the module's one entry into Level 2 of the level ladder.

K8. Three elbow flexors (moment arms $4,3,2\ \mathrm{cm}$; $F_{\max}=500,700,900\ \mathrm N$) share $\tau=10\ \mathrm{N\,m}$. Solve the load-sharing under (a) $\min\sum(F_i/F_{i,\max})^2$ and (b) $\min\sum F_i$, and compare. Probes: §8; two optimisations (a QP and an LP).
Solution
(a) The stress-minimising solution shares force across all three, $\approx(86,126,139)\ \mathrm N$, keeping each at similar relative stress. (b) The effort-minimising problem is a linear program whose optimum sits at a corner: it loads only the muscle with the largest moment arm ($250\ \mathrm N$ in muscle 1, the others zero). Note the totals: $86+126+139=351\ \mathrm N$ against $250\ \mathrm N$, so the min-stress solution spends $40\%$ more total force to hold every muscle at about the same relative stress ($0.17$, $0.18$, $0.15$). The two cost functions give qualitatively different biology, and which the CNS actually uses is an open question — the min-stress prediction matches EMG better, foreshadowing Module 7. 
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import linprog

D = np.array([0.04, 0.03, 0.02])          # moment arms (m)
FM = np.array([500.0, 700.0, 900.0])      # F_max (N)
TAU = 10.0                                # N m

# (a) min sum (F_i/F_i,max)^2 subject to D @ F = TAU: F_i ~ D_i FM_i^2
lam = TAU / np.sum(D**2 * FM**2)
Fq = lam * D * FM**2
print("min stress :", " ".join(f"{f:.0f}" for f in Fq), "N")
print("  relative stress:", " ".join(f"{f:.2f}" for f in Fq / FM))
print(f"  total {Fq.sum():.0f} N, check tau = {Fq @ D:.2f} N m")

# (b) min sum F_i: a linear program, optimum at a vertex
r = linprog(np.ones(3), A_eq=[D], b_eq=[TAU], bounds=[(0, f) for f in FM])
print("min effort :", " ".join(f"{f:.0f}" for f in r.x), "N")
print(f"  total {r.x.sum():.0f} N, check tau = {r.x @ D:.2f} N m")
K9. Using the fatigue model, a target force $F_{\text{hold}}$ is held by raising activation as capacity drains ($a=F_{\text{hold}}/C$), and the hold fails when $a$ reaches $1$. Simulate to failure and report the endurance time as a function of $F_{\text{hold}}/F_{\max}$. Probes: §9; simulate-to-failure + root-finding.
Solution
Substituting $a=F_{\text{hold}}/C$ makes the fatigue equation linear, $\dot C=-F_fF_{\text{hold}}+F_r(1-C)$, so $C(t)=C_\infty+(1-C_\infty)e^{-F_rt}$ with $C_\infty=1-(F_f/F_r)F_{\text{hold}}$, and failure ($a=1$, that is $C=F_{\text{hold}}$) never arrives while $C_\infty\gt F_{\text{hold}}$, that is below $F_{\text{hold}}=F_r/(F_r+F_f)=\mathbf{0.53}$. Above it, solving $C=F_{\text{hold}}$ gives $t=-F_r^{-1}\ln\!\big[(F_{\text{hold}}-C_\infty)/(1-C_\infty)\big]$. The simulation and the closed form agree to the printed digit: 
import numpy as np

FF, FR = 0.018, 0.020          # fatigue and recovery rates (1/s), sec. 9


def endurance(f_hold, dt=0.01, t_max=1e4):
    """Simulate C(t) with a = f_hold / C until a reaches 1."""
    c, t = 1.0, 0.0
    while t < t_max:
        a = min(f_hold / c, 1.0)
        if a >= 1.0:
            return t
        c += dt * (-FF * a * c + FR * (1 - c))
        t += dt
    return np.inf


print(f"sustainable while F_hold < FR/(FR+FF) = {FR / (FR + FF):.2f}")
for f in (0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9):
    t = endurance(f)
    exact = np.inf if f <= FR / (FR + FF) else -np.log(
        (f - (1 - FF * f / FR)) / (FF * f / FR)) / FR
    print(f"F_hold = {f}: simulated {t:8.1f} s, closed form {exact:8.1f} s")

So $\mathbf{67.5\ s}$ at $0.6$, $\mathbf{32.3\ s}$ at $0.7$, $\mathbf{16.3\ s}$ at $0.8$ and $\mathbf{6.6\ s}$ at $0.9$: a $50\%$ rise in the target cuts endurance by a factor of ten. This steep force–endurance curve, absent from any static formula, is the practical signature of fatigue and sets work/rest limits in ergonomics and rehabilitation.

K10. Given a measured twitch (time-to-peak $25\ \mathrm{ms}$, half-relaxation $40\ \mathrm{ms}$) and the calcium-driven model of §3, fit the activation time constant $\tau_a$ by least squares on those two features. Compare the recovered value with the $\tau_a=41\ \mathrm{ms}$ Modelling assumption 3.2 puts into the forward model, and say where the difference comes from. Probes: §3, §5; parameter estimation (inverse fit).
Solution
Minimising $(t_{\text{pk}}-25)^2+(t_{\text{half}}-40)^2$ over $\tau_a$: 
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize_scalar

TR, TD = 3.6, 18.0                  # ms, the calcium pulse of sec. 3
T_PK = TR * np.log(1 + TD / TR)
NORM = (1 - np.exp(-T_PK / TR)) * np.exp(-T_PK / TD)


def twitch(tau_a, dt=0.02, T=400.0):
    """Peak activation, time to peak and half-relaxation time (ms)."""
    t = np.arange(0.0, T, dt)
    y = (1 - np.exp(-t / TR)) * np.exp(-t / TD) / NORM
    ca = 0.1 + 1.3 * y
    tgt = ca**3 / (1 + ca**3)
    a = np.zeros_like(t)
    for i in range(1, len(t)):
        a[i] = a[i - 1] + dt * (tgt[i - 1] - a[i - 1]) / tau_a
    i = a.argmax()
    j = i + int(np.argmax(a[i:] < 0.5 * a.max()))
    return a.max(), t[i], t[j] - t[i]


def cost(tau_a):
    _, t_pk, t_half = twitch(tau_a)
    return (t_pk - 25.0)**2 + (t_half - 40.0)**2


r = minimize_scalar(cost, bounds=(20.0, 80.0), method="bounded")
pk, t_pk, t_half = twitch(r.x)
print(f"fitted tau_a = {r.x:.1f} ms")
print(f"  peak a {pk:.3f}, time to peak {t_pk:.1f} ms, "
      f"half-relaxation {t_half:.1f} ms")
print(f"  forward model of sec. 3 used tau_a = 41.0 ms")

which prints fitted tau_a = 43.7 ms with peak a 0.215, time to peak 25.2 ms, half-relaxation 40.0 ms. So $\boxed{\tau_a\approx43.7\ \mathrm{ms}}$, against the $41.0\ \mathrm{ms}$ Modelling assumption 3.2 assumed — a $6.6\%$ discrepancy, and it is not numerical error (the features move by under $0.05\ \mathrm{ms}$ between step sizes $0.05$ and $0.005\ \mathrm{ms}$). The forward model with $\tau_a=41\ \mathrm{ms}$ produces a half-relaxation of $38.1\ \mathrm{ms}$, not the $40\ \mathrm{ms}$ measured, so the fit lengthens $\tau_a$ until the tail matches and pays for it with a slightly late peak and a slightly low amplitude. Two scalar features are a lossy summary of a whole trace, and both of them also depend on the calcium constants $\tau_r$ and $\tau_d$, which the fit holds fixed; the estimate absorbs part of their contribution into $\tau_a$. That is the general lesson of an inverse fit: what you recover is the parameter conditioned on everything you froze, and reporting it without that condition overstates what the twitch measured. It is nonetheless the bridge to measurement, and exactly how §10’s “how it is measured” works in practice.

K11. Proposition 5.1 makes activation a mass-action binding step for the exposed-site fraction $s$, $\dot s = k^{(3)}_{\text{on}}[\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}]^{3}(1-s) - k_{\text{off}}\,s$, in place of the first-order relaxation of Modelling assumption 3.2. Drive it with the same calcium pulse ($\tau_r = 3.6$, $\tau_d = 18\ \mathrm{ms}$, $0.1\to1.4\ \mu\mathrm M$), with $Ca_{50} = 1\ \mu\mathrm M$ and $n = 3$ frozen so that $k^{(3)}_{\text{on}} = k_{\text{off}}/Ca_{50}^{3}$ and $k_{\text{off}}$ is the one free constant. (a) Show that no $k_{\text{off}}$ reproduces both measured twitch features of K10 (time-to-peak $25\ \mathrm{ms}$, half-relaxation $40\ \mathrm{ms}$): map the pair the model reaches as $k_{\text{off}}$ sweeps $6$–$80\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$. (b) Add one downstream first-order stage, $\dot a = (s - a)/\tau_x$, standing for tropomyosin movement and crossbridge attachment, and fit $(k_{\text{off}}, \tau_x)$ to the two features. Report every solution you find and the peak activation each predicts. (c) Which measurable quantity separates the solutions, and what does the answer say about where the twitch’s slowness lives? Probes: §3, §5; inverse problem with a non-identifiable branch, then model discrimination.
Solution
from itertools import product

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize

TR, TD = 3.6, 18.0                  # ms, the calcium pulse of sec. 3
T_PK = TR*np.log(1 + TD/TR)
NORM = (1 - np.exp(-T_PK/TR))*np.exp(-T_PK/TD)
CA50, N = 1.0, 3                    # frozen, as in K10


def feats(t, a):
    """Peak, time to peak and half-relaxation time (ms)."""
    i = a.argmax()
    j = i + int(np.argmax(a[i:] < 0.5*a[i]))
    return a[i], t[i], t[j] - t[i]


def chain(k_off, tau_x=None, dt=0.02, T=400.0):
    """Ca pulse -> binding s(t) -> optional lag stage -> a(t)."""
    t = np.arange(0.0, T, dt)
    ca = 0.1 + 1.3*(1 - np.exp(-t/TR))*np.exp(-t/TD)/NORM
    r_on = (k_off/CA50**N)*ca**N*1e-3          # per ms
    r_off = k_off*1e-3
    s = np.zeros_like(t)
    a = np.zeros_like(t)
    for i in range(1, len(t)):
        s[i] = s[i-1] + dt*(r_on[i-1]*(1 - s[i-1]) - r_off*s[i-1])
        if tau_x:
            a[i] = a[i-1] + dt*(s[i-1] - a[i-1])/tau_x
    return t, s, (a if tau_x else s)


print("(a) pure binding kinetics, k_off sweep:")
for k_off in (6.0, 10.0, 22.3, 40.0, 80.0):
    pk, tp, th = feats(*chain(k_off)[:2])
    print(f"  k_off {k_off:5.1f}/s: peak {pk:.3f}, "
          f"t_pk {tp:5.1f} ms, t_half {th:5.1f} ms")


def cost(p):
    if min(p) <= 0:
        return 1e6
    _, tp, th = feats(*chain(*p)[::2])
    return (tp - 25.0)**2 + (th - 40.0)**2


for k0, x0 in ((25.0, 10.0), (500.0, 40.0)):
    r = minimize(cost, [k0, x0], method="Nelder-Mead",
                 options=dict(xatol=1e-4, fatol=1e-8))
    pk, tp, th = feats(*chain(*r.x)[::2])
    print(f"(b) from ({k0:.0f}, {x0:.0f}): k_off {r.x[0]:.1f}/s, "
          f"tau_x {r.x[1]:.1f} ms, peak {pk:.3f}, "
          f"t_pk {tp:.1f}, t_half {th:.1f}, residual {r.fun:.1e}")

print("(c) branch A refitted over the frozen constants:")
for N, CA50 in product((2, 3, 4), (0.7, 1.0, 1.5)):
    r = minimize(cost, [30.0, 15.0], method="Nelder-Mead",
                 options=dict(xatol=1e-4, fatol=1e-8))
    pk, tp, th = feats(*chain(*r.x)[::2])
    print(f"  n={N} Ca50={CA50}: k_off {r.x[0]:.1f}/s, "
          f"tau_x {r.x[1]:.1f} ms, peak {pk:.3f}")

(a) The sweep prints, for $k_{\text{off}} = 6$, $10$, $22.3$, $40$, $80\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$: time-to-peak $27.4$, $23.9$, $18.7$, $15.3$, $11.8\ \mathrm{ms}$ and half-relaxation $124.7$, $77.8$, $39.4$, $26.1$, $18.4\ \mathrm{ms}$. The half-relaxation is set by $k_{\text{off}}$ almost alone (the tail is unbinding at resting calcium, Proposition 5.1), and pins it near $22\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$; at that value the kinetic peak arrives at $18.7\ \mathrm{ms}$. To push the peak out to $25\ \mathrm{ms}$ the off-rate must drop below $10\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$, where the tail is already twice too long. The reachable pairs trace the curve in the right panel, and the measured point $(25, 40)$ lies off it: with this calcium pulse, binding kinetics alone is too fast on the rise for its own tail. That is the $19\ \mathrm{ms}$ §5 warned of.

(b) With the lag stage the residual collapses, and there are two ways for it to do so. From the first start the fit converges to branch A: $k_{\text{off}} = 22.3\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ (an unbinding time of $44.8\ \mathrm{ms}$) with $\tau_x = 4.6\ \mathrm{ms}$ — binding slow, the downstream step fast — a peak activation of $\boxed{0.391}$, and a printed residual of $0.0\ \mathrm{ms^2}$ (both features land on their targets at the $0.02\ \mathrm{ms}$ step). From the second start the optimiser runs off to ever larger $k_{\text{off}}$ (the printout shows $3532\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$) with $\tau_x = 43.6\ \mathrm{ms}$, K10’s $43.7$ to the precision of the fit: branch B, binding instantaneous and every millisecond of lag downstream, which is exactly the first-order model K10 fitted, recovered here as a limit, with peak activation $\boxed{0.215}$. Its residual bottoms out at $0.2\ \mathrm{ms^2}$ rather than zero, for the reason K10 already met: with binding removed only $\tau_x$ is left to fit two features, and the peak lands at $25.4\ \mathrm{ms}$. Both branches reproduce $(25, 40)$ to within $0.4\ \mathrm{ms}$; the two timing features cannot tell them apart. The inverse problem is non-identifiable on those data, and a least-squares fit that reported only the branch it happened to land on would have hidden that.

(c) The branches differ by $1.8\times$ in peak activation, and that is measurable as the twitch-to-tetanus force ratio: activation in a fused tetanus saturates at the $a_\infty$ of the sustained calcium, $0.73$ at $1.4\ \mu\mathrm M$ (§4), so branch B predicts a twitch of $0.215/0.73 = 0.29$ of tetanus and branch A one of $0.391/0.73 = 0.53$. Fast mammalian fibres show ratios of about $0.2$–$0.3$; branch B is in range and branch A is not. So, on these constants, the twitch’s slowness lives downstream of calcium binding: the switch itself is fast, as Proposition 5.1 says, and the $40\ \mathrm{ms}$ tail is the crossbridges letting go, not troponin holding on. Two cautions, both the lesson of K10. The verdict is conditioned on what was frozen: the listing’s part (c) refits branch A over $n = 2$–$4$ and $Ca_{50} = 0.7$–$1.5\ \mu\mathrm M$ and prints peaks from $0.113$ to $0.768$ while $k_{\text{off}}$ stays within $21.1$–$27.7\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ — at $Ca_{50} = 1.5\ \mu\mathrm M$ and $n = 3$ the peak is $0.144$ and branch A is no longer excluded. The timing is robust; the discriminator is not. And the model that fits is not thereby the mechanism: a single downstream stage is the smallest addition that closes the gap, not a demonstration that there is only one.

That closes the module. From a nerve impulse at the neuromuscular junction we have built, step by verifiable step, the force a muscle makes and the torque it delivers to a joint — and named honestly what is left for the modules to come.
